They tell me 't is foolish to prate of love In the sweet and olden way; They say I should sing of loftier things, For Love has had his day. But when Dorothy comes I cannot choose, I must follow her Though the world I lose; My very soul Pours forth in song When dainty Dorothy nips along. It is all very well to say to rile fhat tirowning,'s noble strain Rises and swells with the tide of thought Or throbs with the pulse of pain; But if Dorothy once Ilad crossed his path, Her radiance such A witchery hath That across the world Would not seem long To follow Dorothy With his song. .-27a4 Century Magazine.

Time is like a rapid river and a rushing, torrent of all that comes and passes. A thing is nollsooner well come than it is past, and then another is borne after it, and this too will he carried away.—Aurelius:: Books are the food of youth, the delight of old age, the ornament of prosperity, the refuge and comfort of adversity, a delight at borne and no hindrance abroad, companions hy:night, in travelling, in the country. Campbell Foster was once addressing a jury, and was much annoyed by Digby Seymour's carrying on a con- versation the while. Presently he lost patience, and in his best brogue said, Pray, Mr. Saymour, be quiet." "My name is not Saynnour, but Seymour," corrected Digby ; whereupon Foster angrily rejoined, "Then, sir. see more and say less." Mcountryman was standing on one of the wharves the other day watching the process of hoisting an anchor of a ship which was getting under weigh, and as he saw the huge iron rise from the water to the Yo, heave, ho l" of the sailors, he remarked, "You may heave high and heave low, but you will never get that great crooked thing:through that little hole—l know better." AN: UNEXPECTED INSTANCE OF FORBEARANCE.-.—BESSie was dressin,, her doll, while Master Frank, who was out of humor, spoke to her in a very teasing way. She was quick-tempered, but in this instance did not retort. "Bessie," her mamma said, Frank talked very dis- agreeably to you. It was very nice of you not to answer back, as you do sometimes." "Mamma," replied Bessie, "I wanted to, but couldn't. lihad my mouth full of pins." A little Italian girl is in the habit 9f regularly visiting certain houses in Boston, receiving food and other articles, which she stows away in :the basket always brought with her. In her round of visits, one day, she was accompanied by another girl, who had no bisket. The good lady of the house, after supplying the little mendicant's wants as usual, remarked. "Doesn't your companion want something too?" ":0h,:n0," was the reply; "she's rich! Her father works r, An amusing misadventure happened the other day to a well-known artist in Paris. He had purchased an old helmet in a bric-a-brac shop, and when he got hcme the idea occurred to him to try it on. It:went lon easily enough, but when he wanted to take it off he found it impossible to do so. Finally, he was forced to go to a neighbouring gunsmith's to:Thave it removed. His appearance in the street, wearing; this medimval relic, produced a decided sensation. Two lawyers visited the same young lady. One even- ing Jones alone was with her. He said in tender tones, "Do you think, Mary, you could leave father and mother, this pleasant home, with its ease and comforts, and emigrate to the West with a young lawyer who had only his profession to live on, and search out a new home where both could be happy ?" Dropping her head on to Jones's shoulder, the maiden softly whispered, "I think I could, Archy." "Well," said Jones, "there's Tom Brown, who's going to emigrate and wants to get a wife. ru mention it to him." EXTRAORDINARY DISCOVERY OF A RING.--A curious anecdote concerning a ring and a: walking-stick is given in "Notes and Queries." A servant boy was sent into the town with a valuable ring.:He took it out of its box to admire it, and, passing over a plank bridge, let it fall on a muddy bank. Not being able to find it, he ran away to-sea, finally settled in: a colony, made a large fortune,lcame back after many years, and bought the einate on which he had been servant. One day, while walking over his land with a friend, he came to the plank bridge, and there told his story. "I could swear," said he,,pushing his stick into the mud, "to the very Spot on which the ring dropped." When he withdrew his stick, the ring was on the end of it. THE OBSERVANCE OF TUE SABBATH.—Though my hands and my mind have been full of secular business, both before and after I was judge, as, it may be, any man's in England, yet I never wanted time in six days to ripen and tit myself for the business:and employments I had to do, though I borrowed not one minute from the Lord's -day to prepare for it, by study or otherwise. But, on the other hand, if I had at any time borrowed from this dav any time for my secular employment, I found that _ . . . . .

It did further me less;than if a had let it alone; and therefore, when some years' experience upon a most atten- tive and vigilant observation has given me this instruc- tion. I grew peremptorily resolved never in this kind to make a breach upon the Lord's day, which I have now strictly observed for more than 30 years.—Sir 3f. Hale. THE WHITSTABLE " ISATives."—Perhaps the best sea- side place in England in which to see the oyster fatten- ing process is Whitstable. where gravel spread over the blue clay seems:to afford so much nutritive matter that the "fish" increase quickly in size. The human community there does not Increase fast in numbers, and it is said that the reason is that Whitstable forms a very remark- able and exclusive little republic, each member of which has certain rights in the fishery. Strangers are there- fore supposed to be discouraged to settle in the place. Formerly all the sons of freemen in the town were en- titled to be freemen also, and to have their share in all Abe profits ot the oyster dredging, but the eldest son • -vnly is now admitted to the title and its privileges. And very curious privileges they are. You may hear **crier going through the street shouting. "One bushel—Half -tide." And you are told that this mysterious call is the edict of Mcouncil, as potent as the Council:of Ten of old tVeniee, and that it is an order for the freemen who have teats to go outtlat half-tide and tc dredge, but no boat is to bring home more than one bushel 01 oysters. This •-ebuncil that thus promulgates its decrees consists of a mjury" of twelve men, chosen for the year. It;is a bodpthe antiquity of which no man can estimate, for it

baieicisted as lone as there has been any English record AR Whitstable. The Romans knew Whitstable oysters, lint whether they instituted the governing council no man knows. As long as history has acknowledged British insLitutions, it has acknowledged the undoubted rights of the authorities of the little Kentish sea-place. It is their duty to,estimate the state of the market; and -to regulate the catch, as well as to determine all else that helongsto the welfare of the beds out in the shallow Ma, and, -most important of all, to divide the spoils. Now eyes"' .men in this old guild has a right to a" stint," or limited poriou of the value gained, whether he fishes imeelf or isaway at the Antipodes. Alas, now one sees quite as many o-r more of the French oysters here as of the excellent andAicautifully shelled "natives." ; It is only in favourable seasons that a good-," spat" comes Boating on the shalkows of the North Sea, and " hives " of tiles aad other delicate French contrivances are not to be adopted on suds an open line of shore, so that uniess the swimming babies fasten on ;the stuff they tinclAthey are swept away and perish. But there is a c000tt• stool," as the Americans would call the stuff, for them; to fasten upon. Old': clay pipes, among other tbinget are especial favourites, and two or three shells asay be seen engrafted °utiles bowl of a Dutch "church- warden."—Good Word..

The Irish soon find a nickname for everything, and not the least appropriate is that given by them to the present Irish Administration, whom, with reference to their physical peculiarities, they have christened "the shortsighted Government ; " Mr. Balfour, the Lord-Lieutenant, and a good many members of his family all wearing eyeglasses.

The newest freak of fashion, writes a Peri., Cor- respondent, is a looking-glass stand for the menu. Ladies can see how they look at table. Madame Heine took the other day to her daughter, the Princess of Monaco, with whom sheis en a visit at Monaco, four dozen of these mirrors with frames in repouss6 silver of exquisite workmanship. The fashion has come from Russia.

The Queen proposes to go to Edinburgh towards the end of August, when on her way from Osborne to Balmoral, anti her Majesty will then reside for a few days at Holyrood, and will visit both the Edinburgh Exhibition and the Forth Bridge. It is probable that the Empress Frederick will come over to Scotland in the autumn for a few weeks, and her Imperial Majesty will also pay a visit to Edinburgh.

During the closing years of his life, the figure of the late Sir Edward Baines was a familiar one in the streets of Leeds. He retained a surprising degree of vigour ;and elasticity both of body and mind. To the last he preserved his strong interest in the social, politieal, and religious movements with which he had been identified in early life. Down to the end of his life he continued a staunch and consistent teetotaler.

The new Tithe Bill which the Government have prepared differs considerably from that bronght in last year, though its main principle—the abolition of distress for recovery of tithe rent-charge and substitution of recovery through the county court —is retained. Last year the Bill proposed that action might be taken by the creditor on account of tithe-rent in arrear for one month. In the new Bill the arrears must have accumulated for a minimum period of three months.

According to advices frcm Teheran, the little fav- ourite of the Shah, whose appearance excited great interest everywhere during the Shah's visit to Europe. has been betrothed to his Majesty's young- est daughter. In honour of this event the Shah gave a great festival, which in its splendour is said to have surpassed even those mentioned in the "Arabian Nights." Nasr-ed-Din presented his little favourite with his most beautiful estate in the neighbourhood of Teheran. At the same time he handed him a document pronouncing a curse upon any future ruler of Persia who would dare to deprive him of his property.

"Buffalo Bill " feels rather chagrined at President Carnot's refusal to accept a handsome lamp that our famous American had made in America for the French President at a cost of £250. President Carnot declined on the ground that he accepted presents from no one. The lamp is nine feet high. made of carved brass on a table of Mexican onyx 28 inches square. On a plaque of onyx fastened to the lamp rod is attached a large buffalo head, captured by Colonel Cody on the frontiers. The shade of the lamp is 37 inches in diameter, and is made of scar- let silk covered with moss green tulle, embroidered with poppies and corn flowers.

It is safe to say that if the division had followed straight on Mr. Gladstone's speech the Govern- ment would have been beaten. It is an old Parliamentary tradition that votes don't. influence speeches. As a rule they don't ; hut Mr. Gladstone's personal judgment on Mr. Parnell's case,so touching. so moderate, so pathetic in the circumstances and manner of its delivery, struck, for once, a vivid chord of sympathy in all quarters of the House. " E'en the ranks of Tusculum " could scarce forbear to cheer as it concluded, and when Tory members hurried out, two out of every three would have ad- mitted that they had been hard hit.

The Irish members were very much touched by Mr. Gladstone's personal tribute to Mr. Parnell, and the description of his wrongs and sufferings. "That's the first statement of the truth that the House has heard," said one man. Mr. Parnell, too,felt it keenly. though, as usual, he showed no emotion whatsoever, but sat like a stone statue while eloquent reparation was being offered him for unexampled wrong. Sir Charles Russell, however, was more emotional. He wiped his eyes more than once.

Oliver Wendell Holmes thinks that he owes his good health and the retention of his mental vigor in his eighty-first year to the extreme care he has long taken of himself. Never robust, he was still wiry in his earlier and nzaturer life; but since he reached seventy his hygienic vigilance is unceasing. The rooms that he daily occupies are equipped with barometers, thermometers, aerometers—every kind of instrument, in short, to prevent his incurring the slightest risk of taking cold. He knows that pneu- monia is the most formidable foe of old age, and he is determined to keep it at a distance, if possible. He never gets up until he knows tne exact tempera- ture, during winter, or takes his bath without the water accurately tested.

The following incident is related in a private letter in illustration of the steadfastness of the British soldier. When at Gibraltar: Prince Henry climbed the hill, and on approaching the summit at a certain point found himself stopped by a sentinel. "No road this way !" Prince Henry told the man he only wanted to go to the brow of the precipice, so as to see the water on the other side. " No! no thoroughfare !'' replied the sentinel. " But I am the commander of the Irene," said Prince Henry. " All the same; no thoroughfare insisted the soldier. " But I am a Prussian Prince," continued the commander of the Irene. "No thoroughfare !' obdurately replied the sentinel, and Prince Henry abandoned the undertaking.

A funny story reaches us from Dublin Castle. It is well known that the principal firm of Dublin pianoforte makers rejoices in the style and denomi- nation of "Pigott and Company." One evening last week a large party had assembled at the Castle, when one of the Lord Lieutenant's young men pro- posed to start a dance in a room where dancing did not generally take place. A piano was dragged out from a corner and opened in the middle of the vice- regal assembly, when lo! in the centre of the key- board was seed in large gold letters, the fatal words "Pigott and Co." The guests burst out laughing, and with the want of tact that distinguishes the Castle proceedings, the piano was immediately closed, and bundled back into its corner.

The Edmonton Board of Guardians have been engaged in discussing the weighty question of whether it would be lawful to buy a fiddle for a pauper at the expense of the ratepayers. On the one hand the pauper bad pleaded that if he were only the possessor of the coveted instrument his musical talents would suffice to support him. On tl.e other hand, it was not quite clear that the Guardians would be justified in applying the rates to the setting up in business of an itinerant fiddler.

Some derided the whole business, and were heard to ejaculate " Fiddle-de-dee !" and a reverend gentleman, who appeared to be the most sceptical of the assembly, went so far as to observe that " a fiddle" might only mean " a fuddle." Ultimately, the chance of lightening the parochial burdens on such easy terms proved too captivating to be re- sisted; and the difficulty was got over by a volun- tary subscription among the Guardians of a shilling apiece, to be expended, as the proposer put it, "in the acquirement of a violin of the value of the amount raised."

Of late the Czar has been effecting some great economical reforms at his Court, he being annoyed at the terrible waste and frauds which have been perpetrated upon him. " Vanity Fair" gives a few instances. The Emperor has begun with the Civil List. For instance, the allowance to the Empress 'of £OO,OOO a year has been reduced to one half, Whilst also a number of offices have been curtailed, whilst his Majesty's staff has been reduced. When the present Czar ascended the Throne, the Imperial entourage numbered four hundred and five persons, and this has now been reduced to one hundred and forty-three, fifteen being numbers of the Imperial Family. As an example of the manner in which money has been wasted, it may be mentioned that some functionary had been drawing £l5O a year, for" lip salve"! The item attracted notice, and , upon inquiry it was discovered that the man's pre- decessors in office had been drawing this sum ever since the time of Catherine 11., through that august ladyhavimy, once, when suffering fro m chapped lips, ordered a box of the article.

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER NEAR LONDON.
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER NEAR LONDON.

A terrible murder look place on Saturday, in Poplar. Henry Garrod.,a commercial traveller, while alone with his daughter, a child of seven, cut her throat with a razor. No motive is alleged for the deed, but it is stated that the prisoner has for some time been very much de- pressed and strange in his manner.

div.head: N EXPRESS TRAIN WRECKED AT CARLISLE. . FOUR PASSENGERS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.
div.p: N EXPRESS TRAIN WRECKED AT CARLISLE. . FOUR PASSENGERS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.

Early on Tuesday morning an alarming railway acci- dent occurred close to the Citadel Station, Carlisle, to the London and North-Western Scotch express, which left Euston at eight p.m. on Monday night, and which is due to arrive in Carlisle at three a.m. The train was ap- pioaching the station at 3.25, considerably behind its time, when the driver discovered that his brakes would not act. He whistled to warn the guards of this, but the speed at which the express was going could not be materially checked, and the train ran through the station, to the surprise of the porters, who were waiting for it, at the rate of between twenty and thirty miles an hour. The rails were very slippery owing to a fall of sleet, and ' the fireman, not apprehending anything, had made no preparations for discharging sand on the metals. At this critical moment an engine had come from the Caledonian railway shed north of the station, and was proceeding Ito the platform for the purpose of being in readiness for the 420 a.m, north train. Into this engine the express dashed with fearful force. Had the engine been a minute or two sooner or later on its course the collision would not have occurred, but unfortunately the runaway express came up to it at the precise moment when it , was traversing a short section of the down main line in order to get to the No. 1 siding. The line at this spot is straight, and the superior weight of the express sent the Caledonian engine flying back for a long distance, but it did not leave the rails. The first two carriages of the express. however, which were between the engime and a composite sleeping car, were completely telescoped by the collision, and four of the passengers therein were killed and many injured. No part of the train left the rails, but the line was strewe with the wreckage of the two front vehicles. The accident happened about 300 yards north of the station, and the crash was heard by the porters on the platform. They at once rushed down the line, and the work of rescuing the injured was immediately begun. The two damaged carria,-;es were inextricably locked together, and some of the passengers were only liberated after a long delay One lady was only got out after her dress had been cut off. Two doctors who were in the train rendered valuable assist- ance. The ironwork of the carriages was twisted about in the most fantastic fashion, while the front of the engine of the express was battered to bits. The back of the tender also suffered severely, and the first compart- ment of the front carriage—there being no intervening guard's van—was completely smashed. The following is a list of the killed, three of whom , were seated in the third compartment of the first car- riage, and the other in the first compartment of the second carriage :—William Lowles, valet to Colonel Flambro, M.P. Miss Lowson, SEI, Wells-street, London, Walter Ford and Mary Flaxter, servants of Colonel Eyre, Middleton, Richmond, Yorks. The injured, so far as ascertained, are as follows : Thomas Rumney, driver of the express, fractured ribs. Alexander Munro, Chipping Norton, compound fracture of left leg, simple fracture of right leg. Miss Barns, from Stockport, to Inverness, fractured leg. Mr. Har- borne, designer, Grosvenor-rd., London, NW., injury to back and right leg. Miss Harper, from London to Aberfoale, eye cut. Mrs. Ford, Exeter, bruises. Mrs. Flint. Miss Roger, London. Mrs. MiMe, Accrington. Mr. and Mrs Faulkner, from London to Glasgow. Mrs. Ellis, from Cardiff to Arbroath. H. Davis, fireman of the express, Crewe. Archibald Lament, Blair Castle, Blair Athole.

Most of the above are at the County Hotel, Carlisle, but the three first named, whose injuries are more serious, were taken to the Infirmary. Mr. W. B. Low- son, uncle of Miss Lowson, who was killed, was also in- jured. He was travelling north to his father's funeral, and, although complaining of injury to the back, pro- ceeded to Scotland by a later train. Crook, driver of the Caledonian engine, was also slighty injured. After the dead and injured had been extricated, a breakdown gang set to work to clear the line, and by ten o'clock this had been done. The express was made up of car- riages from London and Bristol to Glasgow and Perth, and also carriages from Liverpool and Manchester. Crook, the driver of the Caledonian engine, which was approaching the station when the collision occurred, says Ise was going at a gentle pace and thought the Scotch express had passed.. He was horrified, however, to sec the funnel of its engine appear 40 yards in front of him on the line that he was travelling upon. He im- mediately reversed his engine, but he could not avert the emllision, the force of which threw him back, and ren- dered him insensible. His engine was driven down the incline for half a mile before it could be stopped. His fireman, Campbell, was not much worse for the acci- dent.

div.head: CONDITION OF THE INJURED.
div.p: CONDITION OF THE INJURED.

It was stated on Wednesday evening by Dr. Lediard, who has charge of all the passengers injured in the acci- dent, that most of the :patients at the Infirmary are doing well, though Mr. Munroe, both of whose legs were fractured, is still in a precarions condition. It is not yet certain whether it will net be necessary to resort to amputation, and his life still hangs in the balance. The other very serious case is that of Miss Rogers, who lies in the County Hotel, suffering from bruises, but who has begun to complain of internal pain. It is feared that she received internal injuries whilst hemmed in the carriage. She belongs to Aberdeen, and was travelling from London. Mrs. Ellis, of Arbroath, took food on Wednesday, and the rest are all improving. INQUEST.

The inquest on the four-p-ers-on-S killed by the collision was opened before V.e City Coroner, at Carlisle,on Wed- nesday. Several officials of the London and North- Western Railway were present. The Coroner announced that the Board of Trade had appointed Colonel Bich to inquire into the case. The jury viewed the bodies in the waiting-room, and these were afterwards identified by witnesses as Walter Ford, Mary fluxter, Jeannie Muirhead Lowson, and William Lawless. A witness named Sarah Harper, one of the injured, identified the first two named as her fellow-servants at Colonel Eyre's, of Aberfoyle. With them in the first carriage of the train was another fellow-servant, Elizabeth Flint, also among the injured, and a fifth passenger unknown. Witness was resting her head on Mary Huxter's shoulder when the latter was killed. The inquest was adjourned sine die.

div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.

It's nied sad havoc up an' deawn, I' village an' i' market teawn— Fro' th' pallis reight to th' hut o' t' cleawn, Id dismal presence lends a Sad look to worn mortality; Id grips,—respectin' no degree— At beggars an at Royalty, Thad awful Influenza ! 0 th' doct'rin' tribe grin i' ther sleeve, They know t' use o' good mek-believe, At sich afflictions they dernd grieve, For everyone attends a Fine lot o' gaspin', sufferin' fooak, Till th' ailment geds a conk'rin strooak ; Go wheer yo' will, an neaw is th' jooak— " Hey yo' bed th' Influenza?' Its quite a fashionable thing, For id, like youth, will hey id fling, An' some say t' name's a novel ring Aheawt id; that depends a Gret deol o' whether they've hed th' grip, But raooast contrive to give id t' slip, An' plenty's getten twist o' t' lip Thro' nowt but "Influenza!' It's med a rare excuse for o 'At happens wrong, hi heigh an low; If t' Parish Church clock's fast or Slow; _ _

Or if a fuddler spends a Good share at week-end ov his brass, An' then feels drunken-sick, bi th' mass! He's t' cheek to tell his wife—poor lass, He's getten th' Influenza Neaw t' Monda' slotchers hes id reight, They manage to come eawt on 't streyt, For if they've hed o aleheawse feight, Th' wost pown o' th' pair pretends a Bit o' th' owd sowjer,—Wi'a sigh He'll grunt an' grooan, an' say "Oh my !" An' swears his cut nooase an' black eye Hey come thro' th' Influenza! If mashin' cooarters disagree, lloo'll be i'th' huff—he'll ged on t' spree, An' varra likely mek too free Wi' rum, gin, or "Lochrenza." Then if o' t' Sunda' he's to stop I' bed, wi' his best suit i' pop, O't' Monde' o his mates i'th' shop Gets towd o'er th' Influenza! We've nowt mitch to thank Russia for; I' progress they mek little stor, An' t' wish aw hey—id mut be wor— Is, t' next time th' Emperor sends a Gret howlin' legion ov his pack, To tackle t' good owd Union Jack, May the Russians o' be driven back Wi' tiler own Influenza! div.head: STATE OF IRELAND. FIRING INTO A HOUSE.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND. FIRING INTO A HOUSE.
At eight on Tuesday evening the house of Mr. Binden Blood, J.P., Cranaher, near Ennis, was fired into by a party of Moonlighters. This is said to be the second attempt on Mr. Blood's life.
A CRIMELESS COUNTY.

The Chief Justice of Ireland, at Carlow, on Tuesday, congratulated the grand jury on the very satisfactory condition of the county—he might say almost its abso- lute immunity from crime. The criminal calendar was practically a blank_._

div.head: TIPPERARY EVICTIONS.
div.p: TIPPERARY EVICTIONS.

The eviction campaign was resumed at Tipperary on Monday. Forty-five families are to be evicted, and accommodation has been secured for them by the Ten- ants' Committee. All the houses were cleared before the sheriff arrived, and the evictions are quietly completed. THE RBI 11-BARRY TENANTS. The struggle between Mr. Smith-llarry and his Tipperary tenantry led to a sale at Limerick on Satur- day. Thesub-sheriff seized eleven head of cattle for rent due from a farmer named Oola, and the stock was I put up for auction. -There was a large force of police, and no disturbance occurred, the cattle being bought in for the tenant. . THE CLONGOREY EVICTIONS. The cases of Fathetßinsella and 17 others who had been sent to gaol for illegal assembly after the recent evictions at Clongorey came before the Dublin Court of Queens Bench on Saturday, on the motion for a man- damus to compel IWr..Ye.9ey Fitzgerald, the stipendiary magistrate, to state a case. When the case was called, the Solicitor-General said he had arranged with counsel for the defendants that no rule should be made on the motion, the defendants to be at once discharged from custody. No rule was accordingly made. The prisoners were subsequently liberated, and met with an enthusias- tic reception at Carlow.

div.head: LABOUR AND CAPITAL.
div.p: LABOUR AND CAPITAL.
A deputation from the Belfast section of the Great Northern and Ireland Railway had an interview with the directors on Tuesday in Dublin. It is believed the threatened strike will be averted. _ _ _

The miners' representatives have resolved to hold a conference in Manchester on the 13th inst. in order to see whether the Coalowners' Federation will make an offer to avoid the strike. It has also been decided that if the 10 per cent,advance is offered at any pit the men should be allowi.d to accept it. THE NEW COLLIERIES AT WESTLEIGH. The sinking of the new mines at Westleigh, by the Westleigh Colliery Company, has just been completed. The pits, it is expected, will shortly be at work, and will undoubtedly improve trade in that locality, which has of late not been very brisk. MR. JOHN BURNS ON THE EIGHT HOURS' QUESTION. Mr. John Burns, addresing a meeting of gasworkers and others, at West Hain, on Sunday, declared that the question of eight hours was at the present moment the most vital of all questions. The preliminary vote on the subject in Parliament waslarger than he expected. The eight hours would be only the preliminary measure to enable men to grasp the social problem.

div.head: MEETING OF RAILWAY MEN.
div.p: MEETING OF RAILWAY MEN.

On Sunday ;;;;;;tin.g under the auspices of the Amal- gamated Society of Railway Servants was held in the Public Hall, King-st., Wigan. Mr. Edward Garrity, of Accrington, delivered an address urging the men to com- bine together for their own mutual interest, and the following resolution was passed :—" That this meeting of railway servants heartily approves of the national hours programme set forth by the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, and we hereby pledge ourselves to combine to the utmost extent with a view of carrying such programme into effect."

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

RUNCORN A v. TRANMERE.—Runeorn journeyed to Trantnere on Saturday, to play off their return fixture. Both teams mustered up their full strength. The visi- tors started downhill, and were soon in the home quar- ters, where play was carried on for a considerable time, the home team beingbusy defending their lines, and were forced to save twice in, quick succession. Half time arrived, the score standing two minors to nil in favour of Runcorn. The home team restarted. The game was very fast and exciting, and raging in the Tfanmere half, when Houghton landed a splendid goal from a penalty kick, which gave the visitors a good lead. A grand game ended in a win for the visitors. Final result: Runcorn, one goal, two minors; Tranmere one minor. LEIGH V. WIDNES.—The return fixture between these two clubs was played at Leigh on Satutday. The home teammas without S. Pendlebury, Gregory, and P. Nay- lor. while Widnes was only very poorly represented. Leigh passed well at the commencement,and after a few minutes' play Shovelton got over, no goal resulting. Leigh again got Over, and in a scramble for the ball one of the Leigh men was hurt, a minor only resulting from the drop out. Leigh pressed severely, the backs pass- ing well, the play being in Widnes ground, but the visit- ors defended well. Coop, Smith, and Worthington played well for Leigh, while Parkinson and Brennan were conspicuous for the visitors. lhe game ended in a win for Leigh, by two tries and two minors, to Widnes

WIDNES V. LEIGH " TEAMS.—This fixture was played at Widnes on Saturday, the home team being but poorly represented. Leigh kicked , of, but for a con- siderable time neither side had any advantage, play be- ing of a very even and fast nature. The passing of the home team was a very striking feature of the game, Barber . being particularly prominent in this respect. Wailing received a pass and dropped a neat goal for Leigh. Half time score : Leigh one goal, Widnes two minors. In the second half Mctiurl picked up and passed to Morris, who dropped a splendid goal from a difficult position, thus equalising matters. Immediately after- wards Minton scored an unimproved try. Final score: Widnes, one goal, one try, and five minors, to Leigh one I goal and three minors. RUNCORN V. RIREENERAD PARK.—Forthe second time this season these teams met on Saturday, the return I match being played on the ••Irwell-lane ground, Runcorn, in the presence of about 3,000 spectators. The visitors who were several of their usual men short, started the ball against a strong wind, which interfered to no little extent with their progress. Davies got pos- session of the ball and from a pass by H. Hughes made one of his superb runs and succeeded in getting over without any great difficulty. Brazendale then essayed a goal kick, and the attempt waS a good one, but was unsuccessful. On the resumption of play Lockwood dribbled to Brazendale, and then succeeded a series of splendid passes between Hughes. and Crompton, with the result that the ball was transferred to the visitors' quarters. Then Evans crossed the line; but again the spectators were disappointed, as the attempt at goal was futile. The home team pressed severely but could not break through the defence and at half-time the score was —Runcorn 2 tries 6 minors to niL In the second half Runcorn added another try and five minors, the Park men playing four three-quarter backs and with the wind. A. W. Spence broke through the Runcorn line, and scored a try. Runcorn beseiged the Visitors' goal and eventu- ally. Clarke got over after a magnificient run. At the , conclusion'of hostilities Runcorn had registered 3 tries ' and 11 minors to Birkenhead Park one try. WARRINGTON A v. GRANGR IST.-111 bitterly cold weather this match was played at Warrington, on Saturday. Only a moderate number of spectators had assembled when Grange started the game against a strong wind, and following a spell ef loose play at mid- field, Molyueux handed ever to Jolley, and the last- named giving' Webster.the ball, a try was obtained in the first minute, no goal resulting. The drop out aided Grange to reach midfield, when Lawless was conspicuous by taking play to the visitors' quarters, and after Mullen had tried hard to get away, Daniels smartly eluded his opposing three-quarter and secured another try near the corner flag. Following the kick out a pass from Lawless was intercepted by Eden, and after getting past the quarter flag, handed ever to Briscoe, and only a knock on spoiled an opportunity of a try. After some kicks be- tween the opposing backs' the visiting forwards again came with a rush, Jolley kicking back. Succeeding a series of packs, Grange dribbled to centre, and Jamieson by a smart bit of play, improved the position, and the visitors for a time attacked in the most determined manner, Daniels alone by his smartness averting disaster. Some vied play at this point by Isherwood, Turner, and Eyre of the home forwards, who played a poor' game throughout, was a temporary relief, butjt was only from a bed pass that the home team got to midfield., A long pass from Mather to Daniels enabled that player to get to the quarter flag, and'a kick from Jolley went into touch near the line. It was now Warrington's turn to attack, but the visitors sought relief in a minor. , Moly- neux charged the drop out, and after the visiters had rushed to midfield Barnes forced a minor by a long kick. 'll:'inislanderatanding between' two home players allowed Grange to get to the home quarters, and a kick being charged shortly afterwards placed the home , line in dan- ger. Lawless now put in a geod run, and had be passed a sure try was the result. Hodgson next got clear away. Webster fetching? his maa down splendidly. Jamieson next had a drop at goal afteria good run, but Barnes charged the kick, and a minor was conceeded to the visitors, • half time arriving With Warrington beading by 0-2-2 to 0-0-1. Re-starting play raged at the visitor's quarters, Briscoe finally running round a pack and kick- ing to Barnes, who returned well to touch. Turner now got finely away from a line-out, but Eden tackled his man grandly. 'After sothe. give-and-take play Grange, by the aid of a free kick, invaded the home quarters, where a lot of uninteresting play monopolized the game for a long time. Jolley in the end got away grandly, and after drawing his men, threw beautifully across to Webster, who effected a grand run in, but although tho place was comparatively easy, no goal was placed. A good dribble Jo, Turnec, Eyre, and Isherwood was replied to by Roth, Hugtkes, and Eden, but Warrington shortly afterwards attacked. Exchange kicks followed, and Grange, headed by Hodgson, Fennah, and Jones, rushed to the home territory, Barnes relieving by kicking to touch near centre. hi-and-out play ensued, Molyneux, /Westin, and Howarth on the one side, and Eden and Hughes on the other showing Up. Mather next threw wide to Daniels, who ran well but this was followed by some exceedingly Poor play. Isherwood, owing to a nasty knock, retired, and the home team were consider- ably weakened- Russell then; got away and passed to Webster, whose kick landed play at the 25 flag. Mullin by a couple of dodgy runs neutralized, and from a dribble s. Ed" secured a try; E. Eden kicking a grand goal. Nothing further was scored, and the result of a poor game was Warrington 0-3-2 to 1-0-1. Teams :—War- rington : Barnes, back; Webster, Joney, and Daniels, fine-quarters; Mather and LawleA. half backs ; Catterall, Russell, Molyneux, Eyre, Turner, Isherwood, Johnson, Howarth, and Bate, forwards. Grange: Jones, hack ; Eden, J. Mullin, and I. Mullin, three-quarters ; Briscoe and Jamieson, half backs ; Hughes, Hughes, S. Eden, E. Eden, Ruth, Jones, Mitchell, Fennal, and Hodgson,forwards. ' •

div.head: BOILER EXPLOSION IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: BOILER EXPLOSION IN SCOTLAND.

THREE MEN KILLED. About ten o'clock on Saturday night a boiler explosion took place at Putnpherston Shale Oil Works, MicllotSian, with the result that three men were killed and two in- jured. At the time of the explosion very few men were about the worirs. The boiler was blown some thirty yards from its site, and carried away two large tar tanks with their supports. A large area was strewn with bricks and broken timbers. The men killed were Edward Dempsey, and John Scott, boiler firemen, and Andrew Taylor, retort fireman. Scott's body was found about thirty yards away, while Dempsey was blown to the top of some retorts about 25ft. high, a distance of about 40 yards. Taylor was hurled through the air a long dis- tance over the top of the retorts and across a public road. All the bodies were shockingly mutilated, and the clothing had for the most part disappeared. Tho cause of the disaster is unknown.

IT has not been }landed down to poterity ch was ingenious man that made the cold water d scovery. If ever man deserved a statue, it wilA iie. LZoote people write about 7 ivals or contending enerniec continuing their struggles after falling into the water, but without doubt it is a mistake. It was so then that, after retaining. fierce hold of each other for, a few moments, Martin Woolford and Dick Worrell separated, and each tried his beht to swim to place of safety, but that was easier in design than in fulfilment, for, though they made for and reached the granite embankment, there was nothing to grasp, the tide swept them rapidly along, and after one or twe futile efforts to get at the oruarnental Eons' heads Worrell uttered a hoarse cry for aid. 'Help! Murder!" he cried. This was twice repeated before it talk attention, and meanwhile the young men were both getting •In desperate si,rait. For boats there were none bandy, neither were there any barges moored within reach, and all the while the swift, muddy river bore them on so rapidly that although a stout swimmer, Martin WoMford, incona moded as he was by his clothes, began to feel a chill ing sense of horror. There was a certain amount of good isi his compo- sition after all, for, as Worrell began to cry out hoarsely for help, he made towards hint to try and sustain the struggling man, who was fast losing his nerve and wasting his strength. But no sooner was Martin within reach, than Virorrall made so desperate and paralysing a clutch at him that to have let him retain his hold must ham resulted is the death of both.

Under the circumstances there was no resource then but to strike fiercely and shake the fell..sw off, which Martin did, Worrali's ugly square cheek receiving the blow which sent him under water. The moment he rose he began shrieki3g loudly for help, and heads clustered along the Embankment wall. Some etiolated one thing, some another, but help there was none, though one or two people had the common sense to run ethard as they could owards Waterloo-bridge, in the hope of finding a boat by the pier. • If they had bad to wait for the coming of that boat, however, Martin Woolford's career would that eight have come to an end, and Mr. Richard Worrell have ceased to trouble the suburban race-courses with his presence. Their position was critical in the extv ne, for, b.irne down by the weight of their clothes, swept along and whirled reund by the small eddies of tho ebbi,g tide, t6ey were carried out farther and farther from the Embankment, and were fast growing in visible to the excited crowd, which kept moving casts srd, so as to keep abreast. Worrell had become silent, and after a frantic struggle, ending in his beating the water like a drown- ing Elan, he had gone down, but risen once more, and from the force of habit more than from the use of his presence of mind, he had turned over on his back, and tried to float, while letting himself go with the stream. Martin Woolford swam on close behind.

It was a horrible sensation, and more than once the young man f.-1L as if all was over, and that he might as well let hie leaden arms give wey to the paralysing influence that was weighing them down, for chance of resoue there seemed none. The lamps flashed and twinkled in he black stream, and the shouts of the people upon the Etnbankment sounded distant and strange. Every now and then there was a hoarse thundering in his ears as he sank lower and the water savored them, and at last, darkly looming up in tiont, there was something black that he did not seem to know, but the next moment he saw that it was the bridge. Was he to die?

The idea Deemed horrible, but be was too much stunned and confused to feel the horror very acutely, and the tremendous exertion did its part toward s dulling the pain. His limbs kept on moving meel,•sinically, but he was far deeper in the water than he was at first, and still there was no help. The lights appeared to be dancing now haw." his eyes, and to reel round; the cries on the Ihnbankment were faint, and all seemed to be over; there was nothing but to give up the in- effectual struggle, when suddenly the lights before his eyes were blotted out by something dark, and a vcioe cried to him to "fold en!" - - - -

Then there was the noise of oars, a goad deal of splashing, and directly after he felt himself seized and dragged into a boat. "That was rather near for you, young fellows," said a bluff voice; "we were only just in time." Martin lay panting in the bottom of the boat, feebly beginning to realise that he was in one of the police galleys, and his first words as soon as he could speak were about his companion. "Have you—have you saved him ?" he panted. "Oh, yes; he's all right, I think," said the chief man in the galley. "He's swallowed more water than's good for him, flow came you in ?" "Had a bit of a tussle by the steps, and fell in," said Martin, wm was now shivering so that he could not keep his teeth stilL "Au, wouldn't do it again, then," said the man, gruffly. "We mightn't be so handy next time. There, your mate's all right, you see." For just then, after a few gaeps and catches of the breath, Dick Worrell began to bowl and cry like a great schoo..boy, and in quite as inarticulate a stile. " Here !" said the river sergeant, "take some of this;" and he poured out a little spirit in a flask cup, which Worrell drank with avidity, but with his teeth chattering all the while. " lie tried to murder me, he d id—he shoved me into the river, he did. Take him into custody, policeman. I'll have the law of him, I will." "All right,' said the sergeant; "but don't make quite so much noise about it. Ahoy! Yee. All right. Got 'em both!" he shouted, in answer to a hail from the Embankment, There was a loud cheer from the excited crowd, in the midst of which the galley was rowed swiftly on, and before the excitement had had time to lull, the boat was abreast of the floating station, where Martin soon found himself in a warm bed, and a messenger was sent off for a fresh suit of clothes.

Worrell was close by him, and whenever one of the river policeman was in the room he was laud in his demands that Martin should be taken into custody. " Ile tried to drown me, constable; he t-ied to drown me, that's what he did. Take him off. He ought to be handenffed," "Look here," said the constable'at last, "swot% you have a nap. You'll be better then." "I'm not going to have no nap till he's taken up He's a murderer, that's what he is, policeman." "Yes, he look, like it," said the constable, and he left the place. "I won't rest till I see you tried for 'tempted murder," continued the fellow; "and I'll have my money too. I won't look over this, Martin Vroolford; and if you don't get two years for this ru pay you myself, mark my words." He kept on in this strain for quite an hour, when the restoratives he had imbibed and the exhaustion combined to send him into a deep sleep, in which, however, he kept muttering about " money"—" having the law"—" serving him out "—and the like,. while Martin lay thmking of his adventure, feeling keenly how narrow had been his escape. In the midst of his reveries, his brother Mark arrived with a black bag containing a complete change. Re was flushed and excited, and a look of pleasure crossed his countenance on finding his brother so little the worse.

" You alarmed me terribly, Martin," he raid. " For- tunately your mother does not know. The shock would be too much far her. Row did it happen?" Martin began dressing without a word, but when he bed half finished, his resentment, more than respect for his brother, made him speak. "I got into a squabble with that brute," he amid. ' "But he did not dare—"

—..„ "No, he had been dunning me for money." Mark sighed. "There, you needn't go on like an old woman about A," said the young fellow, brutally. "He didn't dun you. Then we got into a tussle on the ErubsAment, and tripped and fell in. I wish the beast had been drowned.' "If he had you would have been tried for mar.. slaughter," said Mark, quietly. "Good job too. Anything's better than going on 25 we do now." The nervous shock had sent the young man into a state of irritated eiimability, an he went on in an Mused angry way. "It's a wonder I was not drowned; and a pity too,'

HOUSE OF LOBDS.—MOISDAY. The Lord Chaffeellor took his seat on the woolsack at • a guarter-past four. ' LORD SALISBURY AND MR. He detailed the circumstances of his interview with Sir Dighton Prohvn, and emphatically ' denied the statement that he informed ',him that a warrant was to be issued for the arrest of a certain per- son. He conveyed no secret to Sir D.' Probyn, for the best of all possible reasons, that he had-none to convey. The suggestion that Sir D.
