Mr. Webb took the oath and his seat for West Waterford. ADJOURNED DEBATE.—The adjourned debate on the report of the Special Commission was resumed by Mr. Bryce, who expressed his conviction that Mr. Parnell and Mr. Davitt were to be thanked for bringing the Irish question to a head. Sir C. Russell admitted that the judges had performed their functions honestly and impartially; but he could not regard them as free trom prepossess;ons and free from prejudice. Be regarded the whole debate as a bootless and purposeless discussion, and the verdict of the House would be a party one only, given without consideration of the evidence. The Government would by their party vote carry their motion, but it would be at best a Pyrrhic victory, in which they would have displayed neither the qualities of statesmen nor patriots. The Attorney- General followed in reply to some criticisms by Sir C. Russell upon his recent speech dealing with the report. The debate was further continued, and the house ad- journed at five minutes past twelve o'clock.

div.head: ADJOURNED TOWN'S MEETING. THE RESOLUTION DEFEATED: A POLL DEMANDED.
div.p: ADJOURNED TOWN'S MEETING. THE RESOLUTION DEFEATED: A POLL DEMANDED.

The adjourned meeting of owners of property awl ratepayers of Warrington, was held in the Co- operative Hall, Cairo-st., on Monday evening, for the purpose of further considering resolutions passed by the Town Council, and to authorise the Council, to take such steps as they shall deem necessary for promoting a bill in the ensuing session of Parlia- ment to extend the boundaries of the borough, to provide for the purchase of the Waterworks and"to make better provision for the health, local Govern- ment and improvement of the borough, and for other purposes." The Mayor (Alderman Francorah), presided, and there were also present on the plat- form Aldermen Burgess, and Sutton ' • Councillors W. Pierpoint, J. Shaw Green, H. Roberts, J. H. Fleming, W. H. J. Jenkins, Muir, J. Fait-dough, and R. T. Fairclough ; Messrs. J. L. Tunstall, T. Tunstall, J. Walker, W. fl. Brook (Town clerk), and J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk.) The MAYOR read the following resolution which he had moved at the previous meeting :—" That this meeting, as representing the owners and ratepayersof the Borough of Warrington as pursuant to the provisions of the Act of the 35th and 36th Victoria chapter 91, intitule.d An Act to authorise the application of funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in certain cases, approve of and consent to the following resolutions of the Council of the said Borough passed at their meeting held in the Town Hall, Warrington, on the 19th day of December 1889, namely :—" That the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington acting by the Council (hereinafter called the Corporation) do and they are hereby empowered to apply to Parliament in the session of 1.890 for a bill intituled ' a Bill to extend the boundaries Of the borough of Warrington to provide for vesting the undertaking of the Warrington Water Works Company in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington and to make better pro- vision forthe health, local government, and improvement of the Borough and for other purposes. That the costs, charges, and expenses preliminary and incidental to the applying for promoting and passing such Bill into an Act shall be charged upon the Borough Fund and Borough Rate." The Mayor added that Mr. F. Dixon who moved the adjournment of the previous meeting had the right to open that meeting. Before Mr. Dixon addressed the meeting Alderman BURGESS made a slight correction in his speech at the previous meeting. The error he fell into was in giving the result as to the profit to the borough. He did not think at the time that while they would pump the water at Winwick without cost beyond what was being incurred now, they would have to pay for that which came from Vyrnwy. That was the omission, as he did not know the price for the Vyrnwy water. Mr. F. Dixon, who was received with applause, dealt almost entirely with the proposed purchase of the Water- works which he opposed. He alluded to what he con- sidered was the defective character of the water mains, and further objected that the water supplied by the Waterworks Company was altogether too hard for manufacturing purposes. He thought that was not the time when the question of the purchase of the Water- works should have been brought before them. At the present time steps were being taken in Manchester and elsewhere to prevent the pollution of the river, and they might rest assured that Warrington would have to do the same. Water might then be taken from the river for all but domestic purposes, and he did not see why they should not use this water at the baths as well as at other places. (" They cannot do it.") Where was the reason ? (Mr. Diggle "I will show you" and laughter). They all knew that a town should have a good permanent water supply, but was there a man amongst them who could stand up and say that water pumped from the red sandstone would be a permaneht water supply? He did not think there was a man amongst them could stand up and say what quantity of water there was inthat rock. To his mind the water supply from Winwick was of a limited character, and might fail if they were to have a dry season. (Rear, hear.) He did not think this was the time either for the purchase of the Waterworks or for the extension of the borough. They had already burdens enough, and some of them would remember the promises given to them in respect to the gasworks. (Hear, hear.) How many of those promises had been fulfilled ? (" None.") He had not forgotten that Alderman Sutton told them that if they would only give power to purchase the gas works they should have £2,000 a year in reduction of rates, and a reduction of the price of gas. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Dixon then criticised the quality of Warrington gas and particularly that which was supplied to Bold-st., chapel on Sunday night. (A voice: •'lt is everywhere alike.") He asked the audience to tell him of a single instance in which the promises made with regard to the purchase of the gasworks had been fulfilled. (Hear, hear and applause). The MAYOR then invited discussion, and both Alder. man Sutton and Mr. Diggle got up on the platform at the same time. Mr.Diggle, however, gave way. Mclennan SUTTON said he quite agreed with the opinions expressed by various speakers that that bill contained clauses as important as any that could pos- sibly come before them affectingthe borough of Warring- ton, and in the remarks he had to make he should wish it to be distinctly understood that he had no desire to Influence any man contrary to his own convictions. Let every man consider the question fairly and honestly for himself, at the same time he wOuld say let him take the entife responsibility of his own actions and not come forward afterwards and say that he had been forced or persuaded in any way te vote as he did vote. (Hear, hear.) He had considered the question for him- self and he had concluded to give his support to the Bill. With regard to the extension of the borough, he thought that if there were those just outside the boroughwho par- ticipated in all the benefits and enjoyments of ti e town it was only just and reasonable that they should come and pay their proper proportion of the rates. (Hear. I hear.) With regard to the second part of the Bill which dealt with the question of the Waterworks, he was, in the first place, of opinion that it was always desirable that both gas works and Waterworks should be in the hands of the Corporations and that the benefits to be derived from the profits Of those undertakings should belong to ,the ratepayers of the town. (Hear, hear.) Secondly, he thought that for sanitary purpose and for the health of the borough it was necessary they should have an unlimited supply of water at the disposal of the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) That, he thought they would agree, was of the very highest importance. The present supply of water for the flushing of sewers and general sanitary purposes was very scanty, and the want of water had not only prevented them from providing suit- able public baths, such as had been required and

demanded by the town, but they had also been positively compelled to close even the poor paltry and shabby baths that th,y had. (Hear, hear.) Yet they knew that at\ the prese it time there was enough water running to waste Rf Winwick to serve the purposes he had named, if they could have it for nothing. He also alluded to the necessity for a better supply of water to meet the case of fire. One of the arguments, he continued, against purchasing the Waterworks was that the water at Win wick might fail. So might everything fail. (Hear, hoar.) If such an improbable thing as that were to, occur—and he did not think any man in that room would say it was likely to occur—they had a safeguard in the supply they could obtain from Vyrnwy. They should be entitled to a supply of two million gallons per day from Vyrnwy,at sd. per 1,000 gallons,and they could supply that at something like the present price, which was estimated at Bd. per 1,000 gallons, and make a pro- fit of about £B,OOO a year. (Hear' hear.) Another objection was the one alluded to by Councillor Monks the other evening, and he was very much surprised to hear Councillor Monks use it. He said they had no right to purchase the Waterworks without having them 'first examined by a competent engineer. (Hear, hear.) He was surprised that Councillor Monks memory had r failed him so much, for one of the conditions sub- mitted to the Waterworks Company, and submitted at the request of Councillor Monks himself, was that they should have an opportunity, before the pur- chase took place, of avpointing a competent engineer Ito examine the works. ' (Hear, hear.) Why Councillor Monks should have put that forward as an objection to the purchase he (Alderman Sutton) really could not understand. Some people would, no doubt, consider the price it was proposed to pay as too much. ("It is.") But let them put themselves in the position of the shareholders of the Waterworks Company. Would they not, if they were deriving a certain and increasing yearly income from the Waterworks, and were compelled to sell, say, "Give us as much money as will by re- investment afford us the same income that we have at present." And, in the present state of the money market, it would be difficult for any of them to obtain a similar annual income unless they sold their Water works shares at a thirty years' purchase. That was a very serious matter to some of the shareholders, some of whom were perhaps poor widows. (" Oh, oh." and laughter, and a Voice : "Town Councillors.") It was unreasonable for them to expect to buy the Waterworks 1 for less than they were really worth. (Hear, hear.) Referring next to the *sanitary clauses of the Bill, Alierman Sutton said he did not suppose anybody would object to them, as they were of such a beneficial character. With regard to the proposed ex- tension ot the rate under the Public Libraries Act, all he could say was that if they desired to make the library and museum more full and useful than they were it present it would be necessary to go in for this extra rate, as it had already been intimated by the Museum Com- mittee that no less a sum than 2d. in the £ would suffice. ("No, no.") That statement occurred in Mr. Robert Davies' (chairman of the Museum Committee) letter which was circulated and printed in the newspapers. But they must understand that if 2d. was not wanted 10. would only be asked for. He was of opinion that the Bill if passed would be of very great benefit to the town and therefore he must certainly go in for its sup- port. (Applause.) With regard to the remarks of Mr. Dixan as to the promise he (Alderman Sutton) held forth, that, if they purchased the Gasworks they should have £2,000 handed over to the rates, he did not know that he had ever made that promise, but if he had he now confirmed it. (Hear, hear.) They had had more than £2,000 given them from the Gasworks. They had had £BOO in the shape of street lamps besides £l,OOO given over for the benefit of the rates. They had also had a reduction in the price of gas to the extent of Bd. per 1,000 feet. (Hear hoar). That promise had therefore not only been carried out but they had received more than was promised. (Applause). Councillor Muir and Mr. Diggle both rose to address the meeting, and there being cries for Mr. Diggle that gentleman was allowed precedence.

Mr. DIOGLE was considerably interrupted during his speech, the audience being apparently determined to extract some amusement from the occasion. Mr. Diggle was, hewever, in the serious mood and commenced by re- ferring to the great importance of the bill te the borough of Warrington, and added that he was there to give them his views as a practical person in connection with water. There was no water at present either above or below ground in Warrington which was lit for either manufacturing or domestic purposes. In his profession as a managing dver—(A Voice: I thought you were a gentleman," and laughter). Well, he became a gentleman when he became a managing dyer. (Laughter.) The MAYOR asked that the audience should listen to Mr. Diggle, because he was really the most formidable oppo- nent they had on that question. (Laughter.)
Mr. DIGGLE said he was in favour of buying the Water- works, because the town could not get a good supply of water without buying them out ( Oh, oh "and inter- ruption.) " " -
- - , The MAYOR: I would be glad if you will listen to Mr. Diggle for ten minutes ; by that time he will have reached his point. (Laughter.) - •

. , Mr. DIGGLTE, continuing, said he would not have the water either from Winwick or Appleton even as a gift. It would be far better to—(A Voice : " Get drowned" and much laughter.) The reason why he would not have the water was that it would produce effects. like that <producing a piece of pipe coated with lime). (" What is it ?") It was lime, and if the water had that effect upon manufacturers' pipes, how could they expect manufacturers to come amongst them ? War- rington ought to be the largest cotton manufacturing town in the country, and it was because of the water that manufacturers had not stopped amongst them, and the purchase of the Waterworks would not make a fraction of difference on the water. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, Mr. DIGGLE said he in favour of the purchase of the Waterworks, but not at the figure at present offered. By Act of Parliament they could force the Waterworks Company to supply a suitable water,and if they would not supply a suitable water they could force them to give up their Act. (Hear, • hear, and applause.) ' Councillor MUIR said that there were three clauses to which particular attention had to be paid. One was the extension of the borough, which had his entire sympathy; the second was the purchase of the Waterworks, which had not his sympathy, and the third was the Library and Museum rate. Two rates had been named one—of 10. and one of 2d. They must not forget, in justice to the Committee, that it was proposed to create a free library. But the Chairman and the Committee had assured the Corporation and the burgesses that a rate of ltd. was quiet enough, and yet they asked for one of 24. Everyone knew Warrington was sufficiently rated,- and

div.head: 'ME EXA,MLVR, SATURDAY, MARCH 8, 1899
div.p: 'ME EXA,MLVR, SATURDAY, MARCH 8, 1899

if they could save a halfpenny or a penny in perpetuity let them do it. (fakeer, hear.) He knew that the meet- ing would come to It poll, and the sooner it did so the better, for the burgesses of the town would then have an opportunity of sealing the matter., (Applause.) .t • air. JOHN WALHEIR said that he was not quite sure that the best thing would be to get to a poll as quickly as possible It might be better to adjourn again, rather than take upon themselves the heavy burden and serious responsibilities that the Bill' involved. They proposed to take upon themselves responsibility in various clauses of• a Bill that would practically become the Magna Charta of Warrington, and it was desirable that they should know what they were doing, and what they were committing themselves to. He quite agreed with Mr. Muir as to the Library rate. He had been one to agitate the question of freeing the Library for a number ef years. They were told from the beginning that the best way of setting the Library free was to give a rate of another id. in the £. Those who agitated the question did not desire to put the town to the expense of going for a Bill for khalf-penny rate, and they opposed it, but ' when the present Bill was being prepared some of them suggested that they might sink their differences and al- low the half-penny extra tobe included. That was done; hut the half-penny was got so readily from the General Purposes Committee that the Library Committee went further and said—" Let us have another half-penny." (A Voice: The Museum Committee.) It went before the General Purposes Committee, and the Council after- wards. The Chairman of the Library Committee—the gentleman who asked for another halfpenny and now asked fora penny—had admitted that another halfpenny in the pound, while allowing the subscriptions to be abolished, would leave a margin of £9O for the working of the library. His (the speaker's) point was that this was a fair working margin. But the halfpenny rate would bring in £l5 more than was stated, and there was another £l5 to be derived from the £5OO left by Mr. Beaftiont, which brought the margin up to £l2O. That, he thought,was sufficient. (Apple Ise.) They wanted new baths. Would they be surprised when he said the extra halfpenny in the pound that it was proposed to add to the library rate would enable them to have new baths ? If they spent £5,000 on new baths, it would cost, at 3:1 per cent., repaying the sum in 60 years, £260 a year. That meant that they could have new baths for £260 a year. The halfpenny rate would bring in £285 a year, so that they could have the baths with £l5 to spare. (Hear, hear.) Referring to Clause 77 of the Bill, he said it meant that in case of small-pox the authorities would have power to take persons from their homes, put them in temporary lodgings or shelter, not in the fever hospital, and provide a nurse; but it also gave power to charge the sufferers the cost of the nursing. He thought that the Corporation had no right to take power to charge for the nursing. He believed in Paying his way. but when a man had paid his rates, and was taken from his own house for the benefit of the inhabi- tants, it was unjust to ask him to pay again. (Applause.) Clause 77, he urged, should be struck out. Another clause-79—related to the Fever Hospital. Already the Corporation had power to compel people to pay for patients in the Fever Hospital, but it was felt to be so unjust that public opinion protested against it, and that power had for many years not been enforced. Clause 79 was really an extension of the power in question, and if they had already decided not to use that power, in the name of common sense why should they now be asking for more power to do the same thing P When a man had paid in his rates for the support of the Hospital they should not ask him to pay again, and if he had to go to the Hospital in the Interests of the inhabitants let it be free to him. (Ap- plause.) Clause 160 gave power,under certain conditions, to the Corporation to close the Park for certain purposes. If some particular Association wanted the use of the Park the Corporation would have power to close it for a short time. He contended that they had no right to take that power. The Park was a recreation' ground for the tnhobitants, maintained purely and solely by them, and it was an improper thing to close it in the interests of any individual or party. It would be possible, when there was a Mayor's At Home, to say, "We will have a little lawn tennis, and will close the Park." (A Voice : It has been done.) Itt was possible under *tie clause in the Bill, and they should vote against it. (Hear, hear). With regard to the pro- posed purchase of the Waterworks, Mr. Walker said that, after thinking and reading a great deal about the matter, and after looking at what was called the market price of money, he had come to the conclusion that that they must purchase the Waterworks now or never. (Applause, and a voice Never). Alderman Davies sug- gested last week that the gas annuities were at a high figure, and that it was unjust to take them at 25 years' purchase in the Bill. His opinion was that they were worth 28 years' purchase in the open market. That was in reference to securities that were not rising, but the water revenue was a rising one. If a revenue that was not rising was worth 28 years' purchase, was not a revenue that was rising worth more? (Mr. Diggle : If It is a regular rising). He (the Speaker) had gone through the figures for 25 years, and an an average the revenue had risen £323 a year. If that was not a good investment he did not know what was. If 28 years' pur- chase was an equivalent for the gas annuities, they might say they would not pa; more for the water under- takine; ; but an arbitrator, if the matter went to arbit- ration, would take 28 years' purchase as the market price, and, as the Corporation would be compelling the Company to sell, he would, according to rule, add 10 per cent, immediately for compulsory sale. That would at once bring up the price to 30 years' purchase. The shareholders who were looking after their interests would next point to prospective value, and ask the arbitrator to assess it. He would probably give from 10 to 20 per cent, for prospective value. In one instance an arbitra- tor, in the case of Cheltenham, gave for prospective value and compulsory purchase as much as 45 per cent., making an addition to what was considered the market price of £200,000 more than they intended to give. (Hear, hear.) Practically what. used to be 25 years' , purchase WA new 30 years' purchase, the price of money being at present so low. Taking it all round, considering that they had a rising revenue, that it could be easily manipulated in the way of finance, that they might get an extension of time, or a suspension of the Sinking Fund, that £1,200 had already been spent on the Bill, and that delay for another year would add greatly to the cost, they would be doing wisely, if they believed in a" greater Warrington," in beingready for the opportunites which the Ship Canal would bring them. There was a tide in the affairs of towns, as well as of men, which taken at the flood, led on to fortune. They must mind what they were about, and take their tide at the flood. (Applause.) Councillor H. Ronmers consideredthat the speech they had had from his friend Mr. Walker, so far as it advo- cated the purchase of the Waterworks, was the soundest

4 piece of artument they had yet had. (Hear, hear.) He thought also that Mr. Walker had very properly called attention to two serious defects in the Rill in regard to the treatment of persons compulsorily removed to the Hospital or elsewhere for the purpose of public protec- tion. As they had already accepted the principle iliat the town as a whole was to pay for its own protection, and as the principle had worked so well, they could not possibly do better than carry it out .to the full. (Hear, hear.) In regard to the Museum and Library rate he emphatically supported the 2d. as against the rate. They had at present three institutions in Bold-st.—a Library, Museum. and Art Gallery—and it was a matter of pride that those institutions had been managed as well as they had been. (Hear, hear.) It was quite true' that they could make the Library freeona 114. rate, but Ithey must not forget that, besides the abolition of the subscriptions, the growth of the population would of itself bring an extra Beinand for books, and the neces- sity for increasing the library and bringing it up to date. It was no doubt, perfectly right to tell them that they already had a very large number of books in the Library, but a great majority of those volumes were practically unread because they were behind the times. (Hear, hear.) What they wanted to do was not merely to make the Library free, but to have a free Library worthy of the name. They had an excellent !duseem, and they would perhaps be surprised to learn that no fewer than 25,000 people went through the Museum every year. He would willingly spend the whole of the difference between Id. and ltd. rate on the library itself, and he was there to ask for the other half- penny for the Museum. (Hear, hear.) Last year they had only spent about a on the Museum, and this, con- sidering the value of the Museum as an educational insti- tution and the interest that was taken in it by the people of the town, was a contemptibly small sum. (Hear, hear.) They should before very long have to open the institution in Bold-st., on the Sundays. (Hear, hear and "No, no.") He was not going to discuss the question that night as to the propriety or otherwise of opening' Museums on Sundays, but he simplymentioned what he believed to be a fact. As other towns opened their Museums and Libraries for certain hours on Sundays, Warrington would have to f3llow in the wake of those towns. (Applause and" No, no.") They should, how- ever, be prepared to fight the question on its merits when it came forward, and whenever Sunday opening did come it would involve them in additional expense. Then there was the Art Gallery. With the exception of the money left by Mr. Beamont, they had no fund what- ever from which they could purchase from time to time suitable specimens of the work of the artists of the day. He said they had better shut up the Art Gallery alto- gether than keep it as it is. (Hear, hear and "No no.") He thought they ought to put themselves in a position to have a fund from which they would occasionally be able to buy a picture to retain in the institution. (Hear, hear.) In regard to the ques- tion of the purchase of the Waterworks, he was of opinion that the question they had to settle was whether it was desirable in the interests of the people of War- rington that they should purchasa the Waterworks or not. (Cries of " Yes " and "No.") In the first place he would say that the supply of the Waterworks Company was adequate neither as to quantity nor character for manufacturing purposes. Three of the largest works of the town took water from the river, and their action in this matter, which had been facilitated to a great extent by the Corporation, had been the salvation of Warring- ton. (Hear, hear.) The venture which these three works made had been a successful venture, and they were entitled to every credit for it, and as far as he was concerned he would not interfere with what they had done, except so far as would be necessary to protect the interests of ratepayers at large as against the particular interests of those three firms. With regard to the terms of the purchase of the Waterworks, Mr. Walker had put before them in a very clear and distinct way the differ- ence between 28 and 30 years purchase, and he was in favour of the purchase, if everything was as it appeared to be. (flear, hear.) With regard to the question as to whether it was possible Or likely that the water at Winwick could be taken away by coal borings, thel General Purposes Committee should take the highest opinion on this subject, and he believed the directors I were willing that there should be tte completest investi- gation of their property. In dealing with the extension of the borough, Mr. Roberts supported the proposal on the ground that the same precautioris were not taken just outside the borough to prevent the spread of infectious disease as within the borough, and also on the ground that when the Ship Canal is once completed they were likely to h4Ve strong opposition to any extensi .m the Cheshire side from the Canal Company: In conclusion, he again spoke in favour of the twopenny library rate, and remarked that he did not believe they could waste money on institutions like the library and museum. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Councillor W. PIERPOINT said that Mr. Roberts seemed to imply that anybody who 3pposed the library rata of 2d. in the pound was in the position of one trying to stifle the culture and intellectual advancement of the petiole of Warrington. He (Mr. Pierpoint) could, there- fore, not help rising to give some explanation as to why he opposed the raising of the rate to 2d. instead of to ltd. First of all, he was convinced from the discussion that took place in the town, that the usefulness of the Library, Museum, and Art Gallery could be extended even on the penny rate. When the additional halfpenny rate was proposed, he put the question to one of the members of the Museum Committee as to whether a ltd. rate would fulfil all their requirements, and he was told it would. He asked upon whose authority that answer was given, and he was told that it was upon the autho- rity of Mr. Madeley, the curator of the Library. He (Mr. Pierpeint) then sunk his differences, and agreed to the ltd. rate. But the Museum Committee seemed to have been so satisfied with the very easy way in which they got the extra halfpenny that they felt they could not do better than come again. It was always the way : Give easily, and people wanted more. That was the way with the Museum Committee. (Hear, hear' and Alderman Sutton: Not at all.) Well, he had a right' to his opinion. He had asked many members of the Museum Committee why they wanted the extra half- penny, and he should just like to ask Alderman Sutton that question. (Alderman Sutton: Because a halfpenny is net enough" and laughter). Well, Mr. Madeley said ltd. was enough. ("No, no.") He had been assured on ihe authority of Mr. Madeley that it was sufficient and he was inclined to stick to that original idea, and not be led off the scent by what Alderman Sutton said. (Hear, hear and laughter.) His friend Councillor H. Roberts had a bit of a fad for birds—(laughter)—other members of the Museum Committee liked pictures, some would like to see a technical School, and others wanted to have lectures on all kinds of sciences, when they might call in their friend Mr. Diggle. (Laughter.) They also said they would like to teach _cooking, a very sensible thing. (Hear, hear and lauglifier.) Referring to the purchase

a the Waterworks, Mr. Pierpoint said on that subject he followed the lead of his friend Mr. John Walker. Mr. Walker had placed the matter before them in such a clear and yet concise manner that lie need not sav anythisig more than that he endorsed every word that It4t had said. He also believed in the extension of the borough, hut he was against powers being taken to close the park on any occasion. (Hear, heat and applause.) • Alderman BET WYSS here explained that the clauses with regard to the hospital objected to by Mr. Walker were the work of the lawyers, but the Sanitary Authority would take care that there was no charge made for entrance to the hospital. (Hear, hear.) - -

Discussion having been invited by the Mayor, Mr. S. RauLow asked if he might put a question to the Town Clerk, but as it was explained the that gentleman had left the meeting, Mr. Barlow said he would not put the question. Be thought, however, that it was perfectly ridiculous to pay the Waterworks Company thirty years' purchase on their maximum dividends. In answer to a question, Mr. J. L. TUNSTALL explained that there were two ways of providing a sinking fund, by one of which, provided that the income from the Waterworks and the rateable-value of the town remained stationary, the charge upon the rates through the purchase of the Waterworks would at first be Bd. in the pound; by the other way, the charge upon the rates would only be 30. in the pound. Councillor W. IL .T. JENKINS said the clauses in the bill referring to the hospital were, he took it, only intended to apply to such places as proprietary schools, or the Grammar School, for instance. Patients from these places might be treated in our public institutions whose parents did not contribute a penny to the rates, and the clauses would enable the Corporation to recover ex- penses. -

Some discussion then took place as to the mode of putting the resolution to the meeting. The MAYOR said that the Town Clerk had advised him that the resolution must be put to the meeting in full, and either accepted or rejected as it stood. He, however, did not think the clause relating to the closing of the Park should be left in the bill, and he was also against any change being made for treatment at the hospital. Mr. WALKER urged that the opinion of the meeting should be taken on different parts of the bill, and this view was supported by Mr. MAINWARING. Alderman Buitemss explained that the Sanitary Committee would be quite willing to leave out the clauses regarding the hospital. if it was thought better they should be struck ow. (Hear, hear.) The Malcom suggested that the meeting be ad- journed. but Alderman Surrow did not see any good that would be obtained by adjournment. Mr. T. Bitiewszz, said if they put the resolution as a whole they ran the risk of having the whole bill rejected. Councillor T. FLOOD spoke strongly in favour of an inspection of the Waterworks being' made before the purchase was com- pleted. Mr. KIERNAN said the clause relating to the hospital had come upon them as a surprise. He thought they were trying to rush the bill through the mewing. Mr. MAGINN thought they should have had more infor- mation about the Waterwork:t. It seemed to him that everyboay had a special fad of his own, and he suggested they had better adjourn so that at the next meeting they might be told something about the Waterworks. (Laugh- ter and appluase.) The MAYOR ruled that there could be no amendment put to the resolution, but he was willing that an informal expression of opinion should be taken after the resolution had been placed before the meeting. He then put the resolution to the meeting and only about a dozen hands were hel4 up in its favour. There was a great display of hands against it, and it was therefore declared lost.

- - Mr. WALKER then moved that in the opinion of the meeting clauses 77, 79, and lea should be dropped, that clause 61 should be amended so as to limit the library and 'museum rate to 11td., and that, with regard to the purchase of the Waterworks, no agreement should be entered into until there has been an inspection of the Cotnpanvt books by some person or persons appointed by the Corporation, and untilareport has been obtained from a competent water engineer as to the Winwiek and Appleton water supplies, and as to the general condition and prospects of the undertaking. - - - -

Councillor W. PIESPOINT seconded this amendment, which on being put to the meeting was carried by a large majority, only two or three hands being held up against it. Councillor Fx.zulgo said he demanded a poll on the bill. _ .
The MAYOR: A poll having been demanded, the meet- ing is now over. A vote of thanks was then accorded the Mayor, on the motion of Councillor JENK INS.

div.head: OPENING OF THE FORTH BRIDGE.
div.p: OPENING OF THE FORTH BRIDGE.

Large numbers of people left Edinburgh on Tuesday morning to witness the opening of the Forth Bridge by the Prince of Wales. The weather was dull. The Prince of Wales upon his arrival from Dalmeny at the Forth Bridge platform, entered the special train which was in waiting with Lord Tweedale, Lord Colville, Lord Hind- lip, and other directors of the company, along with re- presentatives of the various public bodies both at home. and abroad, including M. Eiffel, the French engineer, and a party of thirty Frenchmen and Austrians. A few minutes' steaming brought the train to the bridge. Away down below crowds of spectators on the river steamers waved their handkerchiefs as they saw the first train lot of passengers steam across the structure. Enter- ing the gaily-bedecked steam launch Dolphin, and followed by the general party in the steamer John Sterling, the Prince sailed out into the Firth and viewed the cantib-ver piers from the water. His Royal Highness seemed struck with all he saw, and expressed his astonishment at the magnitude of the work. Re-entering the train, the Prince returned over the bridge, and on reaching the centre of the northern girder, he completed the bridge by fixing the last rivet. Tnis was done by turning the valve of a hydraulic rivetting machine, and loud cheers from the party, which had mean-time swelled to larger dimen- sions by the arrival of another special train, proclaimed the accomplishment of the operation. The train then took the party to the South cantilever pier, where the Prince declared the bridge open in a few appropriate words. The day's operations were brought to a close bV a luncheon in the model room of the bridge works, which the upholsterer had converted into an elegantly fitted up banqueting hall.

div.head: DOCK STRIKES AT LIVERPOOL.
div.p: DOCK STRIKES AT LIVERPOOL.

There was again great excitement in Liverpool, ion Wednesday. n connection with the dock strikes. About sevan hundred labourers marched in proces- sion to the Liverpool Town Hall with the object of interviewing the Mayor, but his Worship was unable to receive the delegate. The processionists, consisting exclusively of men imported from other towns, then marched to the Workhouse, and were informed by the Vestry Clerk of the conditions upon which alone relief could be granted. On learn- ing that if they entered the Workhouse they could not leave till next day, most of them declined the hospitality of the institutieu, and set off for their homes at Warrington, lianlhester, it. A number of Cornishmen, however, waited on the Mayor of Bootle, and complained bitterly of having been brought to Liverpool by the misrepresentation that their services were required in the construc- tion of a forty-acre dock. The fruit porters of the North-end docks came out on Wednesday for an advance in wages. On Thursday there was an intensification of excitement in and around the Liverpool Docks. About 400 imported men having gone to work at the Bootle and Alexanditt Docks, about 15,000 men congregated around the Alexandra Dock gates, and manifested a determination to interfere, but were restrained by the police. After- wards a procession, alleged to number in the neigh- bourhood of 30,0i10 men, marched into the city through Castle-street, Dale-street, and South John-street. On passing the steamship offices in Water-street vent was given to loud groans. _ _

The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the times of the Romans, since when it has always been popular amongst Western nations. The great mortality of this country, considering its sanitary arrangements, has given birth to a number of shops exclusively for the SALE OF MOURNING. These shops, subsisting entirely on one department, are compelled to charge exorbitant prices, as many a bereaved one is able to testify, having found to her cost, when the funeral was over, that she had made a bad bargain. Whilst making these statements we wish to draw the attention of Ladies to two facts I Thatiwe are manufacturers of Mantles, Costumes. and Millinery, doing a large WHOLESALE TRADE in these departments, and that we supply our customers at the WHOLESALE PRICES. 2. Ours being a general trade with a number of Departments,we are not dependent on our Mourning Trtide for the profits,and can consequently afford to sell at Lower Prices than our competitors. Our designs are copied from the latost Paris and Berlin models, modified to suit the tastes of our various customers. Every Garment is thoroughly examined before being sent out, and for fit, finish, and style we cannot be surpassed, whilst our prices will be found nearly half of those charged elsewhere. During the Sale Special Prices will prevail in this Department. Ladies requiring deep or complimentary Mourning will receive every attention, and they will doubtless be astonished at the value which they receive.

IsEDING 29111 SEPTEMBER, 1890. The Guardians of the Poor of the Runcorn UMOTI are desir- ous of receiving TENDERS from parties willing to contract for the supply of new milk, buttermilk, fresh butter and fresh eggs (for twelve months); flour, oatmeal, groceries, peas,cheese, salt butter ; cod liver and paraffin oil ; quinine; good beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to in- clude about 401bs per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of mutton ' • beat. brand (lets) American or English bacon; potatoes ; wheat straw, drapery and clothing; men's, women's, boy's and girl's shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse. Dutton ; house coal (colliery to be named); coke; good deal coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age, and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; carting at per mile, and funeral at per funeral.—Parties ten- dering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods, will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be ac- companied with samples (except drapery goods), as far as practicable. The GuArdians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter, to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed form of tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various artieles required and further par- ticulars may be obtained. Sealed tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before Saturday, the nod day of March, 1890, endorsed " Tender for----" The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board-room, Dutton, on the 25th March, 1890, at two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written con- tract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, If required by the Guardians. Bv order of the Board, if. LINAKER, Clerk to the Guardians. Frodsham, sth March. 1890.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. MARCH 8, 1890.

Warrington report of the proceedings, The WE must confess to having mad. the oa Tees" Bill. day,of the Warrington Town Council with afeeling of shame and of disappointment; for the Council as a Council began on Tuesday only to openly discuss the Parliamentary Bill of its own creation—a Bill which in one form or another has been before the representatives of the ratepayers for nearly six months. Printed copies of the measure were supplied to members of tbe Council as far back as December 19th, and yet the Bill itself was dealt with by sew of the members as though it was ° thjr first opportunity of discussing with it. Alderlnar BURGESS justly said that "the use of the excuse that they had not even read the Bill" was 'the most idle excuse he had ever heard" ; and fittingly added that "a more humiliating thing could hardly conceive than for members of the Council to say they had not examined the I°2' although they had allowed £l,OOO or 1:1,200 of the ratepayers' money to be thrown away, as would the case if the Bill were withdrawn." We feel' bound to add that such a procrastinatingt• slip-shod way of dealing with the most important business which has ever come before the Warrington Town Council is the reverse d creditable to the Corporation. Even when the members had entered upon a useful discussioia the Bill, they could not proceed with it until it was brought to a legitimate conclusion; for the' meeting melted away until, from lack of a quorutnt no business could be done. And this, too, on the" very night when the Bill itself was actually heinf read in the House of Commons for the seoen" time But we refuse to believe that the 6_7 fathers are really in such a plight as they seen' to be on Tuesday nig'.t. Some of them are, na doubt, more or less interested in the Bill being de- feated; and when a dog is to be beaten any sort of a stick will do. Others again are troubled at the Pres- pect of having to pay a stiff price for the Water Works, as if they were nursing the 101_ hope that a plan might be discovered of gettinF them without having to pay the market price for them. Curiously, not a single member of the Town Coyncil has yet ventured to say that there is acYf question of the desirability of obtaining control o the water supply of the town. The observation is general that, if the works are found, on examinetion, to be in a sound and promising state, they ought to be purchased, if they can be purchased st a fair price. Surely it ought to be possible to determine what is a fair price during the months that must elapse before the bill beconee law; and, with the compulsory clauses droPPeti' there is nothing to prevent the Corporatiee going forward with the bill, and taking P°lcer to buy, or not buy, as may be deemed advisable after due inquiry. Either through ignorance' or timidity, or both, a section of the Town Conn; cil and of the ratepayers are hanging fire, as I voting forthe bill meant that they were irrevocabli and unconditionally committed to buy the.. Water Works at thirty years' purchase. This r not so. The bill is to acquire certain powers: 1311 there is no compulsion to sell—and there is none —there can be no compulsion to buy until a spool' fic agreement has been entered into. As to this, it has already been determined that there shall he no such agreement until the water supply,w orkh?g plant, and general prospects have been satisfak; torily reported on by competent persons. Whit is there then to fear? If the bill pass, the powe", to purchase will have been acquired at .1 large cost; and, if it be thought fit, it Wll, be possible to continue negotiations until neP? year at this time. Even then it would be I)°r_ sible, under the bill, to say—" These Works are not worth 30 years' purchase, and we decline to buy." Decisive action of some kind must be taktet or the ratepayers will be called upon to vote 0 out so much as knowing whether the Corporatio are prepared to back their own bill. It will _b: standing evidence of mismanagement, if th bill is wrecked because there is a difference Of Work opinion as to the value of the Water : ter would be better to drop the whole of the ‘l4 a_ e Works clauses, for the present, rather than l t et h Bill come to nothing. Two is-thirds of 3 loaf _ better than no bread. But, i f the Warr Corporation, after spending £1,200 to acquire roe: powers, refuse even to possess themselves of any will be the powers they have set out to obtain, they inre:. in the position of men who have squiuidered moinoy_ recklessly, and made themselves the bye-wor( every other Corporation in the Kingdom.
I
We have not heard the last of the Lord Salisbury cident which resulted, in the House in a corner. of Commons the other evening, in the suspension of Mr. LABOUCHERE. He has sinned/
I
i
, i
I
I I
It tter the f ig to;

It seems, in venturing to say as to a certain state- ment that he did not believe Lord Sausetray. But what was Mr. LABOUOHERE to do F If he had evidence in his possession which led him to conclude that the PRIatE MINISTER was not telling the truth, he would have been a coward to shirk the issue when it was finally forced upon him. He might have been more polite in intimating his dis- belief in the veracity of Lord SALISBURY; if he has erred, he has erred in being a trifle rude; but that is a small knatter as compared with the charge Mr. LABOUCHERE had to make, namely, that the head of the Government had been party to slefeat- ing the ends of justice by giving timely warning to Lord ARTHUR SOMERSET of the likelihood of a warrant being issued against him. Lord ARTHUR got warning from some one, for he has disappearei, though under suspicion of being guilty of a grave crime, whilst poorer men have been sent to gaol for their share in the same infamous conduct. It is the old story, apparently, of one law for the rich and another for the poor. Lord SALISBURY felt it necessary, on Monday, to give some account of the circumstances under Which he has come to be suspected of being party' to a plan to enable a criminal to escape from jus- tice; and from his own admission there is "some- thing in it," even if that something is not quite all that Mr. LABOUOHERE has been led to suppose. Lord &Tammy says that, by an appointment ar- ranged' by telegraph, he met Sir DIGHTON PROBYN friend of Lord ARTHUR SOMERSET—at the Oheat Northern Railway Station. Lord &tummy his explanation proceeds : " Sir Dighton Probyn came to see me there. He then informed me that what he wanted was to ask Whether there was any ground for certain charges Which had been made in newspapers against sundry persons whom he named. My reply was that, so Sr as I knew, there was no ground whatever, no vestige of evidence, against anyone except one per- son whose name it is not necessary that I should Mention. and I said that as against that person I nnderstood that the evidence was not thought to ne sufficient in the judgment of those whose busi- ness it was to decide. I think I added—l am not pito certain—that rumours had reached me that tnrther evidence had been obtained, but I did not 4nOW what its character was. lam not ashamed to say, My lords, that that is all I recollect of a casual Interview, for which I was not prepared, to which I did net attach the slightest importance, and of Which I took no note whatever. The train started i 7 soon afterwards. The interview was brief and flurried, and, so far as I know, the rest of the Con- Yersation principally consisted in expressions by. Sir Dighton Probyn of absalute disbelief in the Charges levelled against the person 1 have indi- cated, and in answers of a more reserved character on my part." It is just possible we may be doing the PRIME liiNnTER an injustice when we say we think his- lordship is like the lady "Hamlet "—he " doth protest too much." It is inconceivable, as it seems to us, that he should "not attach the slighest importance" to all interview arranged by telegraph, and to a conversation which affected the character in the Meet terrible manner of the son of a duke. What, however, is conceivable is that the incriminated lord should " skeddadle" as soon as information reached him that it was within the knowledge of stbe PRIME MINISTER that "further evidence had been obtained." Mr. LABOUCHERE says it was nederstood that Sir DIGHTON PROBYN WAS to have 'net Lord ARTHUR SOMERSET at a club after the interview; and the member for Northampton was frank enough to admit that if he himself had Obtained information it, a similar way 'as to any friend of his he should probably "have conveyed to him a hint that he would do well to leave the country." But this easy way of treating the matter does not apply to Lord Sews- nurse who had possession of the information as a servant of the State, and who became guilty of a grave offence if he allowedthat information to pass from him knowing that it might be used as a !arning to a criminal to flee from justice. Lord se/am:nee, to put the mildest construction upon his conduct, has betrayed a "plentiful lack" of discretion in giving information to a friend of the accused; and with the knowledge which the coun- try has of other matters which have affected his Character for veracity, he may be annoyed, but he can scarcely be surprised if his explanation is generally looked upon as "another SALISBURY " snmething, that is to say, which is not true. THE action of the Emperor of Ger- „ Labour many in inviting the representativos Question `k. of various European Powers. to a 'nference on the best means of bettering the sondition of the working classes has stimulated an. ;,• .ready keen interest in what, broadly speaking, 3' be termed the labour question. This applies th especial force to Germany and to England the countries which so frequently find themselves 'srPly competing with each other in the markets of the world. The recent elections in Germany ve confirmed what was already previously known, rllely, that there is a seething mass of discontent .'hich is not only making itself heard, but is • ing itself felt lei finding its way into Parlia- l'ent. There is plenty of room in this country for ',"Proving the lot of the workers—particularly 'Ne of the poorer class—but, as we have Often e ,'lnted out, Germany is far behind England; cl it will be something gained if the various "nferences lead to such international action will enable the labourer at home and • t°ad to stand on something like a footing equality. Granted that there is need for a trher shortening of the hours of labour in COUntry, it is not to be denied there 'is much 4,(eater need for taking action in Germany. Mr. ',AS MORRIS, manager of the principal iron teo e r'ts in Warrington, has placed on record his 'Pression of a recent holiday in Germany, and he teal, • es pointed reference to the condition of the' "workers and artizans of Westphalia, as corn- 'e4 with similar classes of workmen in this Speaking first of England he says : ar ironworkers, with a few exceptions, make shir 111q4 ta one week and five another, i.e., they corn- Oil pee the week on a Monday morning, and finish thewtturday afternoon, and those men who work follotiv.e nights one week work the six days the loori,wl9g week. The German on the other hand to d'os 21)E nights one week and six days another, and even. this be commences one week on the Sunday blern. leg and the following week on the Monday to, Ine. terminating the former on Saturday after- 'so'l terminating the latter on Sunday morning. erftek's cruel work for, a forgenian. It is one weary out, and another to come in. with only, every see dunday to call his own. If he happens to live ce• tattee from the works, it becomes one round terNt 4, and bed and walking back and to and fro al- Reel etv. In the case of men who are paid the day, Ervies,,el iths. masons, joiners, and .the building od-.enerally, you will find the comparison not "tvore;,lloee, but astounding. Let us assume the Ottilt hfetime of these- men to be 45 in both et and that they commence to work as lads runio„ ',gm of 14, which practicallk they do in both 1)eopf:3; The German shop rule for such work- leave Is that they commence work at 6. a.m. and 1°,7 4t 7 p.m., taking their meals between 8 and 10 - and 1, and 4to 4.30, or 11 hours work and Week up. for meals, making 66 working hours Fer hilst the bean fr ng with the loss and mischief which result °ln the sys em of compulsory military service in The 'yotuty, Mr. IVIoRRIs says : by the_anner in which the German youth is treated uovernment of his country is, I consider, a

crime. Besides, the treqment does mot affect -the man only, but the manufacturer and capitalist. For just as the youth's experience is becoming ripe and useful, alike to himself and to his employer, partly at the expense of his employer, for he has only been a learner as it were up to this age, he is snatched from his calling, and must join the army—be in the receipt of the munificent sum Of about 4d. per day, and forget what practical knowledge he had acquired during six years of his working life. At the end of the time he is dischalred—sent back to the place he came from, with a back as straight as the gun- barrel he has been handling—and with his ears tingling with the vibration of the superior officer's word of command—with an empty pocket— but thoroughly 'mated up in discipline, and how to smolc,!. tobacco. On the contrary, the English youth at 20 to 23 has just learnt a trade whereby he can earn a respectable living, and assist in support of a , home. He can eat white bread, and have his plea- sures and pastimes, whilst the German mast eat brown bread, and scarcely know the meaning of the word pleasure. Proceeding next to compare the food and lodging of the-English and the German worker, the con- clusion Mr. Monnts comes to is that "the average Englishman spends as much money in his pas- times, pleasures and his religion, as the aver- age German does on the common necessaries of life." We need not wonder, under these cir- cumstances, that there is a loud murmur of discon- tent on the Continent ; for it is not in Germany alone that the continental labourer is over-worked ' and under-paid. It is a move, therefore, in the I right direction for Governments to recognise that something may come of considering these things. Give them time and they may, perhaps,even arrive at the conclusion that an able-bodied man be put to a better occupation than that of killing or get- ting killed. We know at any rate thht the Germans are demanding to know why they cannot have less work and more pay. They are a stage behind Englishmen as yet; but it is to be hoped they will soon "pull up," and enable us in this country to make another step forward in improving the con- dition of the people.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The Secretary of State for War has been deliver- ing himself on the education quespion, and he seems to think that absence of performance may be hidden by a heap of promise. He says they are pledged on the face of the country" to give assisted education; but what of that P "Unre- deemed pledges 's constitute the order of the day with the present Government.

Darwen liss.got the influenza, , and got it "very bad." ,There are no fewer than 1,500 persons laid up out of a population of about 30,000. Parweri lies in a hollow of the East Lancashire hills; and some years ago it suffered terribly, from an epidemic of typhoid fever through the water supply becoming tainted.

There is no ground for supposing that Warring- ton water will prove had; and yet there is reason to fear an epidemic of typhoid; for the sewers, for lack of water to flush them, are "foul as Vulcan's stithy." There is no town in the Kingdom that stands, from its situation, in greater need of sewer cleansing, and it is questionable if there is any town in the Kingdom that gets loss of it. This is one reason, and no small one, why the Corporation should purchase the Water Works.

The Warrington Extension, Water, and Improve- ment Bill was read a second thno on Tuesday, the House resolving: "That it be an instruction to the Committee on the Bill that no provisions shall be assented to which shall have the result of the borough of Warrington being situated in more than one administrative county." This proviso must not be supposed to be a lion in the path, as it is understood that the whole of Warrington— the Latchford portion included—will be reckoned as in Lancashire, whatever the boundary may be.

Two inquests were held at Manchester, on Mon- day, upon children who had been found dead in bed; and there was a case, last week, in Warring- ton. It is satisfactory to hear that there is a prospect of steps being taken to punish parents for these preventible accidents." In Germany, par- ents and nurses are treated as criminals who take children, under two years of age, to bed with them. A similar law in this country is needed. It would be the means of saving the lives of scores of child- ren in the course of a year.

It was a splendid win for Warrington to beat Bournemouth by 34 points. on Saturday, in the competition for the Challenge Shield of the National Physical Recreation Society. It is especially encouraging as following upon the vic- tory over the London team. But the homesters must beware even of success; it sometimes leads to over-confidence and slackened effort. There must be none of that, if they would be victorious in the end as at the beginning.

Medical men have a pretty free hand in charg- ing, hut they cannot do as they like. In a case heard at the Liverpool Court of Passage, on Tues- day, a bill of 232 17s. ed. for attendance on a wor- king-man was reduced to £2O. And quite right, too. It is uncommon, however, for cases of this kind to come into court. As a matter of fact, it is much more common for doctors to get nothing for their services. They work hard, as a rule, amongst the poor, and frequently forego their fees.

Mr. Labouchere's " suspension " is not by any means a case of suspended animation. On the contrary, he is just now particularly animated. He made a palpable hit," on Saturday evening, in re- ferring to the incident. He said:—" Why was he suspended? The House of Commons seemed to think that the members for Northampton should be very believing men. The House of Commons not many years ago expelled his colleague because he did not believe in things heavenly; they sus- pended him (Mr. Labouchere) because he would not believe in things of the earth, earthy."

St. Minorite election has proved to be another " " for the Tories, and it is all the mote sig- nificant, coining as it does so soon after the issue of the Report of the Parnell Commission. At the election of 1886, the Conservative majority was 261; to-day the boot is on the other lea ; the Liberals have a majority of 108. The transference of votes is about the average of the bye elections; and carried through a General Election it would return Mr. Gladstone to power with a large majority at his back.

Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, calls attention in our correspondence columns to the necessity of keepibg a watchful eye on statements of accounts as to public charities. It is unquestionable that many charities have, through irregularity or over- sight, been lost to the public. It seems that with regard to parochial charities the accounts require to be entered upon the minutes of the Vestry book, and presented to the Vestry meeting. This is of moment, and should be seen to at the approaching Vestry meetings. Mr. Handley quotes the Act, so that inquirers may be armed with authority.

The Chairman of the Newton • Improvement Commissioners was quite right in objecting to a record of minutes which might convey a wrong impression of what he had said at the previous meeting. How could he have intended to say Mr. Pearson went to London to lay charges against him, when in the same speech he remarked that Mr. Pearson had not the manliness to go him- self? That meant that it was somebody else who was acting on Mr. Pearson's behalf. When there is a doubt as to the form of expression, it is always safer to depend on the sequence of thought.

The Chairman has been subject to a good deal of annoyance as superintendent of the Earlestown Railway Works ; but ,it is as well to remember that Sir Richard Moon completely exonerated him as to the unfounded charge that was brought against him. Speaking at the half-yearly,meeting on February 21, Sir Richard, referring to gr. Emmett's protest against the unjust attack upon him, said : " Tbey had also had great complaints of the

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Hannon, of 9, Water-st., was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly, and doing wilful damage to a drum, to the amount of 145., on Saturday, the Ist inst.—P. C. Crane deposed that at five o'clock on Saturday afternoon, he found the prisoner drunk and disorderly in Barn-st., Widnes, where a large crowd had gathered around him. There were two musicians playing in the street, and the defendant had deliberately put his' foot through the end of the drum. He was behaving in a disorderly manner. --Sergeant Wilcox deposed to being in the office when the prisoner was brought in by the last witness Inspec- tor Keighley said the prisoner had been up before the Court 30 times previously, for various offences, includ- ing felony, assaults, and drunkenness. The Bench fined him 10s. and costs or 14 days, for being drunk and dis- orderly, and 10s. and costs and 14s. damages for the second offence, or go to goal for 14 days, one sentence to follow the other, _ .

TRH MUZZLING ORDER AT RUNCORN. Mr. Walter Collier,gmcer and provision dealer, Church- st., appeared before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. P.C. Hulse gave evidence to support the charge, and stated that the dog ran across the street from the shop. The, defendant said he went from the shop to speak to his carter and '‘.lte dog, which was a rough haired terrier, followed at his heels. Retold the carter to carry the animal inside, and he did so, and the constable never saw the dog until it was in the man's arms. Mr. Reynolds said it was attaining the law a little to say that a little dog that had just escaped from the house across the street was at large. They must not attempt to compel owners to keep their dogs muzzled in the house altogether. A little latitude should be given and they should give it in this case, and dismissed it.— A fine al' ed., and costs Bs. ed. was imposed upon each of the following for breaches Of the muzzling order : William Osborne, Ashridge-st. (whose wife said it was not dogs but policemen who ouzlit to be muzzled) ; Frederick Packer. Dixon, Halton ; William Hall, Runcorn; and Itihn Williams, Clifton. ALLEGRD SUNDAT TRADING AT RUNCORN.

To answer a Summons, charging him with having exercised his worldly calling on the Lord's Day, William Rawlinson, greengrocer, Delph Bridge, appeared before the Runcorn magistrates, on Mmuday. P.C. The defence was a tete denial, and witnesses were called to show that the navvies had asked for apples, but as there were neither apple i nor oranges in the shop they were not served. The herb beer was drawn for ilie defendant's son.—The Bench held that there was no proof that the articles were sold, and dismissed the case. Prom our advertising columns it wilt be seen that Runcorn will be visited en Thuridav next by the Rev. Thomas Champness, the editor of "Joyful News." Mis- sionary enterprise is a characteristic of the Wesleyan Methodist body, and in Mr. Champness is typified mis- sionary spirit of no ordinary kind: He is the founder of one of the most important missions in the Wesleyan Methodist Connexion, and sustains it in a very vigorous existence by the prosts of his newspaper, and by such voluntary subscriptions' as are forwarded to Idm. tinder his control are Aunt a nundred men anitwomen who carry on valuable religious 'work in the towns and vil- lages, where their services are needed, and they can point to many extraordinary Successes in spreading a true knowledge of the Gospel. In Rochlale,Mr. Champ- ness has founded a home for these missionaries, who, when not actively engaged. take up their residence there and have the services of an efficient tutor to employ their leisure. On the occasion of his visit to Runcorn on Thursday next, Mr. Champness will preach in St. Paul's Chapel in the afternoon, and in the evening he will ad- dress a meeting in the same place: He is a most effective preacher and public speaker, his views being set forth in quaint and expressive diction, and doubtless lie will attract crowded audiences by the unique position he hasgained in the Wesleyan body. MARRIAGE AT WIDNES. • A marriage, in which more than ordinary interest was manifested, was solemised at Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, on Wednesday, when Mr. Herbert Hutchinson Nield, of Widnes, son Of the Rev. Joseph Nield, Wesleyan minister of Bardney, was united to Miss Jane Sadler, eldest daughter of Mr. Samuel Sadler, of Chestnut Lodge, Ditton. The ceremony was witnessed by &large number of spectators, every seat in the sacruddifice being occupied. As thr guests assembled, Mr. Joseph Robinson played suitable selections on the organ, aid at 2 o'clock the bride entered leaning on the arm of her, father. She was attired in a dress of cream cashmere and cream moire silk, set off with sprays of orange blossoms, and the attendant bridesmaids (Miss Minnie Sadler, Mia Flerrie Sadler, and Miss Nield) wore dresses of silver grey cashmere, trimmed with moire silk, and hats to match. The bride and bridesmaids carried bouquets of choice flowers. Mr. J. H. Nield, brother of the bride- groom, acted as best man. The Rev. Joseph Nield, father of the bridegroom, conducted the service, assisted by the Revs. T. Law, and CT. S. Meek. The service was full choral ; and at the, conclusion Mendelsohn's .• Wedding March" was played on the organ. After- wards the wedding party partook of lunch at the hods° of the bride's lather and later in the day the happy couple departed for Llangollen for the honeymoon. The presents were valuable and numerous.

div.head: INNOCENT IRISH RAILWAY TRAVELLERS IT WIDNES.
div.p: INNOCENT IRISH RAILWAY TRAVELLERS IT WIDNES.

On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, John McGloyne, John McDermot, and Anthony Philbin, all of Castlebar, Ireland, wereea.ch charged with travelling on the Lon- don and North-Western Railway from Chester to Ditton, on Saturday, the Ist inst., without, having obtained a ticket.—Mr. W. J. Bland, from thesolicitor's°department, Lime-street, Station. represented the railway company, and said the three prisoners arrived at Ditton by the 7.10 train from Chester on Saturday. On alighting from the train they asked the stationmaster which was the plat form for Wigan, and they were directed to the other side of the line. They went up the stairs as if to cross the line, and instead of going on No. 3 platform, as directed by the stationmaster, they gave up their tickets to the booking clerk at the door from Castlebarto Chester. The collec- tor, on examining the tickets, called the defendants back, and got hold of Philbin, who pushed him away, and they all ran away through the fields. The booking clerk in- formed the stationmaster of what occurred, and a porter was sent after them. They were traced to Halebank, Tarbuck, Wootton, and latterly to Cronton, where they were arrested in a public-house.—The defendants ad- mitted the offence, and pleaded that they made a mis- take in getting theirtickets, and understood the fare was the same to Ditton from Castlebar as to Chester. The prisoners were each fined is. and costs, and Philbin was further fined Is. and costs for resisting theclerk, Richard Hughes. A brother to McDermot paid the fine and the prisoners were released. • ALLEGED THEFT OF A RUG NEAR RI:MODEM. - - - • --

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, Arthur Jones, a respectably dressed young man employed as a grocers' assistant,was charged with having on the 26th February, at Little Leigh. stolen a horse rug worth 2s. Bd., the pro- perty of James Maddock, a labourer of that place. Mr. A. Linaker defended. It was alleged that on the afternoon of the day named the prosecutor and a farmer named William Brock were engaged in ploughing a small field by the road side, and had placed the rug in the field about ten yards from the gate. The defendant drove up in a spring cart, alighted, opened the gate, and picking up the rug, quickly returned to the cart and drove away, although both men shouted to him to stop and" drop the rag." Brock went in pursuit, and came up with the defendant at Mr. Rigby's, the Heath Farm, Little Leigh. Ile asked him why he took the rug, and he replied that he thought it was lost and he was going to advertise it. Brock said nothing of the sort, as he must have seen or heard two men in the field, whereupon the defendant cursed him. P.S. Dutton on Saturday apprehended the defendant, who then said he found the rug pn the hedge.—For the defence Mr. Linaker stated the defendant bad been in the employ of a respectable tradesman of the town for seven yea rs,and his employer had the greatest confidence and trust in him When driving round by Little Leigh for orders on the day in question he saw the old horse rug, which was not worth more dun a shilling, lying on the roadside near a gate, and thinking It was lost and might belong to Mr. Rigby, at whose house he intended to call, he picked it up. He had no felonious intent, and when Mr. Brock charged him with stealing it, he naturally resented the accusation. Mr. Linaker eon- . tended that the case had not been made out.—Mr. , Reynolds said the magistrates thought the defendant had taken what did not belong to him, and they were'sorry. to see so respectable a young man in ,stleil a position. They had decided to let him off on payment of costs ZI Bs., and hoped he would never do anything in the future to forfeit the confidence of his employer.

Our readers will learn with feelings of deep regret of the death of the Rev. George Bright Bennett, who was from 1864 to 1870 perpetual curate of Holy Trinity, Run- corn. Notwithstanding the refusal of the Treasury authorities to advance .the funds for the purchase •of the range at Glazebrook, there is every probability that the scheme will be proceeded with. The site is such all extremely suitable one and is so convenient that a strong effort to acquire it will be made by the commanding officers of the six regi- ments concerned. An appeal will probably be made to the friends of the volunteer movement in this district, and it is not at all unlikely that a military bazaar on a large scale will be held for the purpose of raising the greater part of the mousy required.
A WIFE DESERT= 22 YBARS AGO.

A singular case of wife desertion was heard at the Prescot Petty Sessions, before Messrs. F. W. Hare and 11. R. d'A. Willis, on Tuesday. Joshua Sumner, an elderly man, who had been apprehended at Bolton, was charged with deserting his wife, whereby she became chargeable to the Prescot Union. The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and said his wife bad turned him out.—Mr. Stuart, relieving officer, stated that the prisoner's wife Isecame chargeable to the Union on the Ist January last. in consequence of his desertion at a former period. She was nOw in receipt of reliet.—The prisoner said he had not lived with his wife for over :20 years. —The Clerk (Mr. Spencely): When did this Man go away ?—Mr. Stuart said he had not positive know- ledge, but he believed it was twenty-two years ago 1 when he left to avoid a serious ,charge.—the Clerk said the warrant wa, against the mart for deserting his wife on the Ist January last, but it appeared he did not desert her then.—Mr. Stuart said that was. the date when the wife become chargeable to the authorities.—The Clerk said that had nothing to do with it.—Mr. Stuart : llis Wife has been relieved to the extent of .E 17.. from that, period up to now.— The Bench tool that the prisoner would be dis., charged, and lie Must be.brought up beforetheru on another charge.

Sonic interest- has been itCx-c-i-t-e-d-in St. Helens by the announcement that Mr. Charles Kincaid, who, nearly three years ago, resided in that town as the United States Consul, has been apprehended in con- nect ion with an extraorlina-y affair at Washington, U.S.A. Mr. Kincaid iN the ashington comspon- dent of the " Louisville Titres," and in the •course of his correspondence to that j mrnal be appears to have written something which irritated Mr. William Faulbec, formerly a member of the Hou*s of Repre- sentatives for Kentucky. The two gentlemen met in the corridor, outside the door of the House, on Friday, when a ijolent altercation took place between them. Mr. Faulbec pulled Mr. Kincaid's ears, but .the door keeper separated them. The quarrel then ceased for a time, but was resumed shortly afterwards. Mr. Faulbec again attacked Mr. Kincaid and pulled his nose, where- upon Mr. Kincaid, in accordance with the almost universal custom prevailing in Kentucky, pulled out his revolver and shot his assailant. The bullet entered the right side of the head, close to the eye, and is believed to have lodged behind the right ear. Several persons in the vicinity at once at- tended to Mr. Faulbec, whose wound was a danger- ous one, and Mr. Kincaid was arrested on a charge of assault with intent to murder. Later telegrams stated that Mr. Faulbec is progressing favourably, and that Mr. Kincaid has been released On bail. Last October Mr. Kincaid paid a short visit to. En- gland on commercial business, and paid a visit to St. Helens, where he stayed for about seven days. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at an hours' uotice.—J. W. Duttou. Sinks y-street.

div.head: TILE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: TILE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer reported that the numberof deaths registered during the past month rtsvemted to thirty nine. Of these nine were due to bronchitis, two tochild- birth, three to phthisis, three to inflammatien of the lungs, five to senile decay, two to cancer, two to premature birth, two to abscesses, five to mesenteric disease, two to heart disease, and one each to pleurisy and rheumatic fever. The above deaths showed an averazze death rate of 28 per 1,000 per annum of the estimated nopulation. No case of notifiable disease had been reported for three weeks. .
