div.p: PARLIAMENTARY AND LEGAL BUSINESS.

Mr. Wiswall proposed that the following resolutions, passed on the sth December, 1883, be rescinded, "That every Committee of the Board shall refer all business involving le al proceedings to the Parliamentary and Legal Comeattee. "That in cases of infringements of the Market and Lodging-house byelaws, the inspectors, with the advice of the Committee and the Law Clerk, I,;t empowered to to take proceedings in urgent cases."— Mr. Wiswall said this appeared to be a, cumbersome Imode of proceeding, especially as the Highway and the Health Committee consisted of the whole of the members of the Board, and moreover, the resolutions were not I acted upon.—Mr. Hankinson seconded the motion.—Mr. Speakman, chairman of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee, said that Committee was appointed because 1 there was a laxity in regard to legal matters, and in one case in particular, a small maVer grew Ito such proportions, that it cost the Board £1,500. The Committee was constituted for the protection of he Board, and if the Board rescinded the resolutions, the members would not act wisely.— Mr. Smith supported Mr. Wiswall. He WYS not aware that the members of the Committee had had any special training in legal and Parliamentary matters, any more than the rest of the members. (Applause.)—After further discussion, the motion was carried by ten votes to two, the minority being Mr. Speakman and Mr. Meadowcroft. IMPORTANT CONCESSION BY THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY,

The Parliamentary and Legal Committee.—(a) Recom- mended that the agreement dated the 17th day of June, 1885, made between Daniel Adamson and Henry Boddington of the one part, and the Irnprovtment Com- missioners for the town of Runcorn of the other part be cancelled, and the rights of the Commissioners in respect of the land at the ends of King and Mersey-streets be surrendered, and the closing of Castle Rock-road not opposed on the following terms :—The Manchester Ship Canal Company shalt agree to make the following new works and alterations in works and to give the facilities hereinafter mentioned— (l).—To make and maintain a new Graving Dock at or near the Old Quay, Runcorn, in accordance with the plan submitted by Mr. Leader Williams, in November, 1889, such Dock to be contructed within twelve months

ot the opening of the Ship Canal. (2).—To increase the width of the Lock entrince from the River to the Canal at the Duke's Dock, authorized work 1 G (c), five feet, viz. :—from 40 to 45 feet. (3).—The said Company to give an undertaking to improve the present Dock accommodation at the Duke's pock and the access thereto, if, after the opening of the Ship Canal they find it desirable and practicable to carry out such work. (4.) The Company to allow the Commissioners or their contractors during the construction 'of the Ship Canal (a) the free use of the Bridgewater Canal for the carriage of night soil, ashpit refuse, street sweepings, &c.' in boats belonging to or hired by the Commissioners or their con- tractors: (b) the free use of tipping maces at the Stone Croft and at the end of Ellesmere-st.--the use of such tipping places and the locks to be subject to conditions to be set forth in the agreement.—(s.) The Company at all times hereafter to provide a tip or wharf having a frontage of 70 feet at the least at some point between the Ferry Slip and Mersey-at. on the Ship Canal, the position of such tip or wharf between the said Ferry Slip and Mersey-st. to lee changed at the requirement of the Company, and to allow the Commissioners or their con- tractors to load night soil, &c., into boats at such a tip or wharf on the Ship Canal subject to bye- laws to be hereafter agreed upon. The Commissioners to pay to the Company the annual rent of one shilling.— (6). In the event of the Commissioners purchasing a plot of land east of Mersey-st. and within the town boundary to beused as a night soil tip or depot and in the event of the Company owning a strip of land I between the Ship Canal and any land wiich may be I purchased by the Commissioners for such a purpose the Company to give facilities for access to the Canal on reasonable terms to enable the Commissioners to take advantage of section 62 of the Manchester Snip Canal Act, 1885. Any differences between the said parties as to the said terms and facilities to be settled in manner pro- vided by the said section 62. It was also recommended that the sum of £2 17s. 4d. be paid, being expenses of deputation waiting upon the Directors of the Manches- ter Ship Canal Co., in Manchester on the 28th ultimo. The Board went into Committee to consider these minutes, and on resuming they were passed on the pro- position of Mr. Speakman seconded by Mr. Taylor.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Mr. Joseph Pritchard pre- sided, and there were present the Rev. A. M. Wood, Rev. Dr. Ga.staldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, J. J. Howitt, and' G. Moss (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL ATTEHDANCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTEHDANCE.

The Committee had interviewed 82 parents of children who were not attending school regularly, and were suit- ably dealt with. The Committee ordered that seven parents be summoned before the magistrates. The re- ports of the School Attendance Officers were read, and showed that there was a decrease of 50 in the average school attendance, and of the per centage from 80 to 78, as compared wiT h the corresponding period last year. The reason assigned for the decrease was the prevalence of influenza, which had affected all the schools simul- taneously.

The Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £277 45., including £lBl on loan account. The Clerk submitted an estimate of the money required meet current expenses of the Board up to August next, when the school grants were received. After making the pay-menu recommended, there would be an overdraft of £9B attributable to the cost of the election. The, requirements were estimated at £536, making a total of £834. From this is to be deducted £lBO, esti- mated receipts for school fees, leaving a b-dance of £454 to be provided. The Committee recommended that a precept for £450 be served upon the overseers for halt- year ending September 29th, 1890.—The minutes were approved, and the precept signed. TECHNICAL EDUCATION. _ _ _ I

The Clerk reported that the Committee had considered the question of adopting the Technical Education Act, 1889, and the subject was adjourned until the members had made themselves familiar with the provisions of the Act.

---FREE EDUCATION.—IMPORTANT DISCUSSION. The next business was the notice of motion by Mr. Flowitt on the subject of Free Education. Mr. Howitt ' wished to divide his resolution into two parts and con- sider first, "That this Board petition Parliament to enact that education in all public elementary schools be free from all chare,."—The Chairman said this course could not: be pursued without notice, except the mem- bers consented. Dr. MaDoneall anti Dr. Gastaldi objected. and Mr. Iro*itt moved that the Board peti- tion Parliament to enact that education in all public elementary schools be free from all charges, and that all schools in receipt of grants from Government be under direct representative management. Mr. Howitt said it was unneceseazy for him to make a long eeeecli oe this subject, imiemuch as every member of the Board was acquainted with what had been stated by abler men in the Howe., of Commons, and the party in 'favour of Free Education was s:renger than ever was pee:, eted at this time. A resolution similar ta the one lie propOsed had been adopted by the London School Beard. When they considered that all children were compelled by Act of Parliament to go to public elementary schools, he thought the doors ought to be opened, and the children admitted :without asking the parents for any money. If parents were poor he was aware that they could apply to the Guardians, who could remit fees, but it was a humiliat- ing position to put parents into, and he objected to this ! system, which would cease If the schools were made 11 free. He pointed out that vaccination was compulsory ! and the law had provided that parents could have their children vaccinated free of charge, and education ought to be more open than vaccination. He thought no gentleman could be opposed to free education on a sound basis. The second part of the resolution was rather more difficult to deal with. He knew his friend Dr. Gastaldi and the Vicar would not be willing that the ratepayers should assist in the management of their schools. but the day had come when all schools that receieted State aid would have to be under the con- trol of the public who paid the rates, and therefore dis- cretion was the better part of valour ; they had better take the thing in hand so far as the Board was concerned ' and petition Parliament in the terms of his resolution. ! He related an instance of how the present system of ! school fees pressed heavily on poor people, and said if !free education was adopted the average aineunt would eilly be 4s. 6d, per annum for every male abore 21 years of age.—Mr. Taylor seconded the proposition. He had not, he said, considered the question as thoroughly as he should like to, because it was a comparatively new thing, but he thought that before long it would come very forcibly before the country. Be did not know whether Parliament would see its way to enact as far as Mr. Flowitt's resolution went, but he believed there was plenty of room . for improvement at pre.4ent. On the !previous night there were many distressing cases before I the Committee. A child of poor parents had been en- well and unable to attend school. When the child (lid return to school the officer admitted that an advaneed fee was demanded. He considered this very unjust indeed, and there were several of this kind of cage. The Board had no power to interfere with the maneeement of these schools, but he maintained that as these schools received grants from the Imperial Government they ought to be placed under public control.— Dr. Gastaldi said the motion was altogether misleading, tending if properly interpreted to bring over England a fatal collapse as regarded her natural and noble aspira- tions. If by free education was meant the final divorce ot religion from secular education or vice versa, then such a principle was an evil and a fiend to the English realm and its loyal constitutions. Christianity was the synonym of progress, and the European and all civilized countries owed their perfection in constant pro- gress to the influence of true Christianity. Why then should they debar it fromlour own centres? Why should I they desire to attack the foundations and remodel the ! whole building by advocating a principle which would undoubtedly in years to come destroy Christianity from our midst. By adopting free education in England as advocated by the Secularist party they would level h-r to the rank of a Republic without a sing or a nation bereft of social respect, conscious of acting righteously by feeding countless pigs with the substance of countless babies fearing that it might cost too much to rear and educate them. He maintained that free education must go hand in hand with the principle of Christianity, and on this' basis he was ready to accept the principle of free education if by the same was meant a compulsory law that every child should be educated without the penalty of paying the miserable fee of 2d. to 6d. as the lease may be, per week, for his learning • provided that those who had the charge of Christian education should be left free with the management of their own schools, subject to the local authority as regarded their financial , statements. On these terms he professed himself a pro- moter of free elementary education, inasmuch as a ' tremendous inequality existed between Board and Voluntary Schools. In England and Wales in 1889 the expenditure per scholar in average attendance had been £1 16s. 4d. in Voluntary Schools, whereas for the Board schools it had been £2 4s. 7a4. Moreover, whilst the Voluntary Schools contributed 6s. 7ed. out of their Voluntary subscriptions the Board Schools had received 17s. 71d. each from the rates ; and whilst the Volun- tary Schools obtained 17s. led. per head from the tiovernm.nt grant, the Board Schools had received 18s. 14d. per head. itsides,Board Schools had borrowed en the security of the rates the awful amount of £20,678,877 for 1,807 schools to aCcommodata 1,654,061 scholars, the estimated cost being thus £l2 10s. for each child. In England and Wales there were 19,328 schools; of these 14,659 were voluntary schools, and 45,62 were Board schools : hence if the principle of free education was to beceine a fait accomplie, the enormous expendi- ture of between $0 and 60 million pounds would be necessary t) come out of the rates ; besides the sum necessary ter the maintenance of the schools under the plea of free education, they were throwing dust in the eyes of the ratepayers, that becoming blind to the miser- able voluntary pay of twopence or more per week to educate their chilaren, they would grind them down and compel them irrevocably to pay an augment of Bd. or Is. in the £ in emrpetuum whether or not they had children requiring education. The speaker pointed out that during the past year the sum of £2,631,393 was contri- buted from the rates to the support of Board schools and nil to the voluntary schools, while the scholars in the latter passed an equally good examina- tion, and concluded by contending that free education ' would be a burden on the poor ratepayers.—The Vicar
n 5

moved an amendment that it is undesirable for this Board to express any opinion upon the free education question, until some practical measure has been laid be- fore the legislature and the country. He was not dis- posed to think that everybody had made up their minds that free education was desirable in itself. Most thought- ful people were open to conviction in the matter. It had been said that taking away the expense from parents for the education of their children was a questionable step. It was evident that if all schools were free, there would he very little choice of schools, and that probably many private adventure schools would spring up all over the. country. A number of parents would not like to send their children to schools that everybody went to, that if they were all open there would be no distinction, and it might be a very serious question whether education would not deteriorate instead of advance for that reason only. Besides that, were they prepared to support free education from the bottom to the top? Were they to have free education right through the great schools, or were they to have a hard and fast line. There were a great many difficulties, and these difficulties would have to be thoroughly considered in the House of Commons, and before the country, and until that had been done, it seemed premature to petition in favour of the matter. No satisfactory scheme had been put before the country. He pointed out that several plans proposed would result in the abolition of the voluntary schools, and said if a plan could be brought forward which would not inter- fere with the religious instruction given, then it was very likely that it might be accepted by everybody. If the only way of making schools free involved the extinction of the denominational schools, it would mean such an enormous expenditure. In Runeorn, if the voluntary schoOls were shut up, he gave the figures of a calculation .showing that the increased expenditure would mean a rate of Is. 4P. If it did not come from the local rates, but from Imperial sources, they would still have to pay in some shape or forts. Were they prepared to petition Parliament to enact a Bill by which they would have to pay Is. 41d. in the £ more for the benefit of our educa- tion? He thought the Board ought to be a body for administration rather than a body for discussing these kind of things, which they had no power to carry out.— Dr. McDougall seconded the amendment.—The Chairman said the suhject had been discussed in Parliament and definitely postponed for this session, and he thought it was unnecessary and out of place to petition Parlia- ment at the present time. They learned by the discus- sion in Parliament that all parties were favourable to free education. (Hear, hear.) The principle had been accepted by the Government and the Opposi- tion, and the subject only awaited a favourable opportunity for passing a Bill through Parliament. The question of how free education was to be applied was an all-important and complicated subject. In addition to that free education was somewhat para- doxical, for money would have to be provided for the amount of fees that were to be abolished, about £l,Boo,ooo.—Mr. Howitt said there was nobody who could define to him how the system was to be carried out, and how the money was to be got. The money would have to be had, and all the figures compiled by the Vicar and Dr. Gastaldi did not amount to a snap of the fingers, because there were figures he could have assumed quite contrary.—The Chairman said the correctness of the figures could be ascertained if necessary. What- ever amount was received by public elementary schools would have to be provided out of local rates or Imperial taxes. He mentioned various difficulties in the way of free education, and said until the matter was elevated out of the crude uncertain condition in which it was at present., he shoted hold himself uncommitted, so that he might be in a position to approve or oppose the proposed enactment on the subject.—Dr. McDougall, in speaking in favour of the amendment, said Mr. Howitt ought to have given more substantial reasons why they should adopt his resolution.—The Chairman explained the method by which school fees were remitted now, and said last year there was paid in free education in Runcorn £55 3s. 3d. Of that amount Ell as. sd. was remitted by that Board for children attending their own schools, and £45 Os. 10d. VMS paid by the Guardians for a free education of poor children in voluntary schools.—Mr. Howitt, in summing up the die- cussion, remarked that the Vicar had said that they had no experience of free education. There was nobody ought to be better able to tell them something about that than Dr. McDougall. The country that was an honour to him, and he hoped that he was an hoeour to the country, had free education. In Scotland they had free education. Not only was elementary education free, but the Universities of Scotland were also to all intenta and purposes fiee, and he knew that the ablest men that Scotland or the world had ever produced, had been educated at the Universities free of charge.— Dr. McDougall said he had to pay for his. —Mr. H twitt also mentioned that they had free education in Germany, America, and Switzerland.—On the amendment being put to the meeting it was carried by four votes to two. For—the Vicar, Dr. Ciastaldi, Dr. McDougall, , and the Chairman. Against—Mr. Hewitt and Mr. Taylor—The Chairman declared Mr. Howitt's motion lost.

div.p: SPECIFIC SITIIIKTS.

div.head: BACK FROM TilE GRAVE.
div.p: BACK FROM TilE GRAVE.
•A. WONGE2FUL STORY, AS RELATED BT A BIRMINGHAM
MOTHER.

(Birmingham Saturday Night.) Our representative called the other afternoon upon Mrs. Durrant, of 79, Camp Bill, Birmingham' with re- ference to a strangely wonderful case in which her son had been a prominent figure. Our representative was received with great politeness by the mistress of the , house, a pleasant motherly-looking lady. On mentioning the nature of our business, we were immediately shown into a cosy, comfortably-furnished parlour, where we remained for nearly two hours, listening with engrossed interest to the marvellous story of how Thomas Currant was literally Brought Back from the Grave. "My son, Thomas Stephen Durrant," began the good lady, will be 19 years old on the 4th March. Although sever a sturdy, robust lad, he still up to the middle of last year had been in the enjoyment of fairly good health. By profession lie is a clerk, having for between nye and six years been in the employment of Messrs. E. R. Pearce and Co.' 104, Great Charleest., Birming- ham. Owing to the death of the head of the firm last year, he had to seek out another situation, being next engaged as junior cl3rk at Messrs. Grainger Smith and Walter. of Carrs-lane, Birmingham. It was when he tad been at this situation for about three weeks that the symptoms of the ailment first showed themselves from -which he has since been so great a sufferer." Mrs. Durrant here paused for a minute or so before recom- •mencing her narrative. "I am afraid," she at last began, in a voice tremulous with emotion, "that the majority of people who read this marvellous story concerning my son will entertain great doubts as to the genuine- ness of the case I am about to lay before you. I can very well understand them doing so, for at times even I hardly seem able to realise that my dear boy, after passing through so much suffering, has really been safely 'brought back from the valley of the shadow of death. Ilowever, in order to give the curious or unbelieving a full opportunity of testing the accuracy of my statement, I give dates and addresses, and whenever practicable, names too. You will understand that in some cases I c,ould not give names, without causing great annoyance and offence to worthy gentlemen whose feelings I would not willingly' hurt. Otherwise I have nothing I desire to conceal, indeed shall only,be to glad too give all the publicity I can to the case, if but to show my gratitude for the wonderful manner in which my son Was rescued from death.

...... " It was in the early part of June last that Tom first began to feel unwell. He became aware of a swelling in the ankles and round the eyes, while a few days after this he was also afflicted with a glandular swelling. Without being in any actual pain,he soon became affected with an unusual sensation of langour and heaviness. For a week or so he remained at his employment, but as his legs continued to swell, he was at last compelled to desist from his occupation. On Saturday, June 23rd, he went home and took to his bed, where he remained until *Tuesday morning. On that day he went to the Queen's Hospital with a view of becoming an out-patient. The surgeon, after having examined him, immediately re- commended that he should at once go into the institution. *My son assenting, he remained at the hospital for 10 weeks and 2 days. During that period he' underwent several operations and apparently all possible was done for him. Despite the fact that his legs were punctured and he went through a regular course of medicine, he kept getting worse, swelling so much that he could not leave his bed. " At length," here the mother's voice became broken as she recalled the mental agony and anxiety of the past few months, "one day on going to the hospital I was Informed that my poor lad had better be transferred to the General Hospital, and from there to the Jaffray Suburban. On making inquiries as to the reasons of this step, the doctor said that they haddone all that lay in their power to save him, and that they could see very little -chance of his recovery. He told me that Tom was filling rapidly and might die at any minute, that he had Bright's Disease in its worst form, and that little else than a miracle could save his life. "Even while he had been lying in the hospital under their treatment I had often thought I should like to try a remedy of which I had read in Saturday Night, a journal ever welcome in our happy home. While I thought my son was progressing favourably I restrained my desire to do this, for who was I that I should pre- sume to dictate to properly-qualified practitioners as to what medical course should or should not be adopted! When, however, they practically admitted their inability to cure poor Torn, I determined no longer to resist my 'convictions, but made up my mind to give that far-famed medicine a trial of which I had read a 3 much in the pages of 13irmingham's popular week-end paper. "Immediately on Tom's arrival home, he commenced taking " Warner's • Safe' Cure, and obeying their dietic instructions, which I found to my surprise were totally at variance with the hospital directions. Notwithstand- ing this, however, I persisted in the course laid down by Warner's. There was no appreciable difference observ- able in the lad during the first week, but on Saturday, September 21st, he was seized with convulsions, which, on passing off, left him entirely blind. About four O'clock on the same day, he had another attack which entirely took away his speech. A doctor whom I called in informed ma that my son could not possibly last the night through. He was altogether unconscious for three days, after which I again commenced giving him Warner's 'Safe' Cure. By the end of the week he had partially regained both sight and memory. I still kept the doctor in attendance upon my son, as I feared in case of his death some trouble might arise. Notwith- standing this, I am in a position to most solemnly aver that from the time that Tom left the Hospital, on September sth, up to the present day he has taken no ' medicine whatever except. Warner's • Safe' Cure. _. .

On Saturday, October sth, at mid-day, he had another convulsion, which left him completely paralysed all down his left side. "From this period," continued the good lady, "my Sou commenced mending. The water began to °disperse from the abdomen first, then from the legs, and lastly from the paralysed parts. As the weeks went by he Continued to improve until, on Christmas Day, by the aid of a stick, he was actually able to crawl downstairs and eat his Christmas dinner with the rest of the family. Meanwhile. the paralysis had also been gradually leaving him, until now, at the present time, it has entirely gone. "But come in and see for yourself ," said Mrs. Durrant, and we followed her into an adjoining room, where, re- clining in an arm-chair, by the brightly glowing fire, v;as young Thomas Durrant. He rose as our representa- tive entered the room, and, stepping forward a couple of paces, offered us a thin white hand by way of wel- come. He had the pale, worn look of one who had been to the very threshold of the Shadow Portals, but a smile lighted his face, and his quiet voice had a cheerful ring, as he thanked us for coming. Speaking of his marvel- lous recovery, he joined with his mother in expressing to us his sense of the great debt of gratitude he owed to his deliverers from death. His last words ere we passed from the room, will never fade from our memory: I was given up by the doctors six months ago as incur- able—dying. When they could stretch out no helping hand. I found a benefactor greater than them all. I turned from them in despair, only to be snatched from the very brink of the grave by Warner's 'Sate' Cure. In publishing the above interview, Mr. J. C. Ilawkes, the editor of Saturday Night, says "In another column will be found a full account of

, bow Thomas Durrant was brought "flack from the Grave." Tile story is told in vivid language, and for the benefit of similar sufferers I think it only just and fitting that I should here remark that of my own personal knowledge, I can vouch for the truth of every word in the narrative of this most marvellous cure. The lad is well known to all the members of the staff of this paper, and his recovery has been watched by us with the very keenest interest."

The Warrington tnagis-rates, on Monday, fined John McOwen, of 4, Friars-lane, off Friars-green, ss. and costs for keeping an unregistered lodging-house. Inspector Nornrin proved the case, and said the houge was adapted tor six, and when he visited it on the 23rd February he -found 13 in persons in it—six members of the family and -seven lodgers. The house was dirty and was unfit to be registered.

div.head: HEARTLESS FATHER SFET TO PRISON.
div.p: A HEARTLESS FATHER SFET TO PRISON.

On Wednesday morning, at the Warrington Police Court. Thomas Hart, a bill-poster, who had been appre- hended in Liverpool on the day before by Constable Chantler, was charged with having run away from the Borough on the 11th February, leaving his two children chargeable to the common fund of the Union. llr. Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guar- dians, said that after prisoner left the town his children became chargeable, but his wife had been supported by her mother. The, magistrates sent Bart to prison for a month, with hard labour. AN IMPUDENT CASE OF ROBBERY.

On Tuesday. at the Warrington Polee Court, a dis- reputable woman named BEM Smith was brought up in custody on a charge of having stolen a half-sovereign from the vest pocket of Charles BartOn,a bricksetter, who lives at Latchford, and works on the Ship Canal. On Sunday evening Barton was in Mersey-st., and was accosted by Use prisoner. Be alleged that while speaking to him she took the coin from his pocket. She was apprehended on Monday, when she had between eight and nine shillings In her possession. Prisoner,who denied the offence, was sent to prison for a montth, with hard labour." It was ber 38th appearance before the Court.

div.head: WIFE ASSAULT.
div.p: WIFE ASSAULT.

John McEvoy, a labourer, who in Wellington-st., was brought before the magistrates at Warrington, on Tuesday, on a charge of having assaulted his wife, on the Ist inst. 'She said that had it not been for two men who were in the house at the time he would have killed her. As it was, he kicked her and tried to choke her.

Defendant called evidence to the effect that he only attempted to kick his wife, and that his foot did not reach her. The magistrates came to the conclusion that an assault had been committed, and imposed a fine of 203. and costs, or a month's imprisonment in default.

A DRUNERN MAN ASSAULTS A POLICIMAN. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday morning, a labourer, of no settled'abode, named John Williams. was brought up on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly at Bridge-foot, at nine o'clock on the previous night, and having assaulted Constable Davies whilst act- ing in the execution of his duty. The officer said that when he went to the prisoner to apprehend him on a charge of being drunk and disorderly, he struck him on the chest. They fell, and while on file floor the prisoner kicked him. Constable Critchley came to his assistance, and the prisoner was locked up. Prisoner, who said he remembered nothing about the matter, was fined 103. and costs.

COAL TIPPING IN TRE STREETS. Robert Anderton, th, landlord of the Cross Revs. Buttermarket-street, appeared at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, to answer a summons alleging that on the 25th ult he allowed a load of coals to be tipped in Buttermarket-street, after nine o'clock in the morn- ing, contrary to the bye-lawsof the Borough. He nleaded guilty, but added that he was in ignorance of the bye- law in question, and that the coals had been tipped be- fore he was aware of the fact. It was stated that the bye-law did not apply to the back streets of the town— only to the four principal streets, namely, Biittermarket- street, Sankey-street, Bridge-street, and Horsemarket- street. The mayor said the defendant would be called upon to pay the cost of the summons, 3s. 6d.—Defend- ant: I shall have to read the bye-laws more carefully.

A CHESTER 'RAILWAY SERVANT'S ADVENTURE. On Wednesday morning the Warrington magistrates had before them a young man named Stanton, who lives at Chester, anal is a fireman employed on the Great Western Railway. He was charged with having, on the afternoon previous, trespassed on the railway near Bank Quay Station, and with having assaulted a signal- man named Cleg.g. Mr. Ashurst, stationmaster at Bank Quay. raceived a telephonic message from the signal box near Ditton's Mill, to the effect that 'a man was there breaking the windows and interfering with the signal- man. Witness and a platelayer went to the box, and ascertained that the man had struck the pointsman, and had gone down the line in the direction of Liverpool. He was brought back, and locked up. Clegg, the signal- man, said that prisoner appeared to have been drugged, and the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that when he was brought to the police-station he had a wild appear- ance, and all the symptoms of having been drugged. Prisoner, it transpired, had been to Manchester with a train, and came back, according to instructions, hy a passenger train. He received a very good character, and told the magistrates that he only had one glass of beer when in Manchester. Under these circumstances the case was not pressed, and the magistrates only directed that he should pay the costs, ene shilling.

THE OTHER WAY ABOUT. "Wife assaults" are.but two often heard of, but a "husband assault" is not 'so common. A case of this sort was, however, heard at the Warrington Police Court on Saturday, Catherine Hudson, of Hardy-st.. being sum- moned by her husband, an India rubber worker, for hav- ing assaulted him. Hudson stated that on going into his house on the 26th February, the "first thing that came at him" was a brass candlestick which was broken in two. His wife, it appeared, was a victim to drink. On the previous day his wife sold a table and three chairs, and pledged other goods in the house, in fact, "every- thing she could lay her hands upon." She was drinking continually. The wages he gave her on the previous Saturday had been spent, and there had been no food in the house all the week, although "he had had to work early and late." They had been married between 14 and 15 years, but his wife had only taken to drink within the past four or five years. In the year 1887 a separation order was granted to his wife, but as he could not obtain his pension under those circumstances he and his wife agreed to live together. He obtained his pen- sion, amounting to about £ll, but his wife snent it all in about a month.—Alderman Burgess : Is this the first time she has assaulted von P—Complainant : No, sir. During the first week of the present year she struck me on the head with a poker.—lnspector Cox said the defen- dant was a very drunken woman, and Constable Jones said the other day she rendered herself liable to be locked up.—She was fined 10s. and costs ; in default of pay- ment to go to prison for 14 days, with hard labour.

THE CORPOR4TIONBILL.—THE TOWN CLERK AND MS CLIENTS. At a mectipg of the General Purposes Cpmmittee, a report (previously published) of the Sub-Committee appointed to negotiate with the Warrington Waterworks Compapy for, the purchase of their undertaking was adopted. Among resolutions adopted by the-Commictee, which have been given in previous issues of the "Examiner," was ene to the effect that the sum of five hundred popncls, on account of Parliamentary Costs already incurred, in connection with the Corporation Bill, be allowed, and a cheque for same forwarded to the Town Clerk's London Agents. The estimated expenditure of the Committee for the year commencing 261 h March, 1899, amounted to a total of £2,188 14. 4d. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman Surrox seconded the confirmation df theminutes. THE TOWN CLERK RETAHrbD BY OPPONENTS OF rars BILL. Councillor HENRY ROBERT& said he wished to•move as an amendment that the minutes of the General Phr- poses Committee be confirmed with the exception of the resolution to the effect "That a sum of £5OO on account of Parliamentary costs already incurred be allowed, and a cheque for same forwarded to the,Town Clerk's London agents." He moved that amendment after very careful consideration, because he was anxious that the Council should have before them, if possible, some proof of the I indebtedness of the Corporation to the Town Clerlee London agents, and in order that comparison might be I made between the charges so incurred and what would be considered equitable and fair charges. He was told that for the printing of the Bill alone a sum of £lBO was I charged by the Town Clerk'SLondon agents. ("Shame.") I He had been told also, on practical authority, that a sum of £4O or £5O would be a fair sum to pay for such work. If that was the case, comment was needless. He had been told further that something like 209 guineas was charged for Counsel's fees in drafting the Bill—a sum, in his opinion, altogether out of reason sad pro- portion to the amount of work done. (Hear, hear.) He had another reason for moving that amendment. He was informed that a certain number of petitions had been lodged against the Bill. He was informed also that a certain petition had been presented, and that the brief in connection with that petition hadbeen accepted by the present Town Clerk to the Corporation. H that was the case—well,he could congratulate those gentlemen who had been astute enough to enaage the services of the Town Clerk in that capacity, but he could not con- gratulate the Town Clerk upon his fidelity to his first employers—the Corporation and the ratepayers of War- rington. If the statement was correct, the Council. were ' entitled to an explanation, and if it was correct the sooner the services of the Town, Clerk was dispensed , with the better. They could not,, in justice to them- ' selves and the ratepayers, go to the-serious matter of a poll with a Town Clerk engaged, on the one hand,, in prosecuting the interests of the Cceporatioa as their legal representative ; and, on the other hand, fighting against it as the accredited agent of one of their oppo- nents. (Hear, hear.)

The Town. CLE RR said he must rise to explain hie posi- tion. (Hear, hear.) In the first place the London agents were not his Parliamentary agents, .but the Parliainen- tory agentibt the Corporation ;.and the whole of those costs, before they were paid would be subject to taxa- tion by the. proper authority. Therefore, there- was nothing to be said about that. With regard to the second matter his services as Town Clerk wouli cease on the 25th March. He cared not if they ceased at once, for the matter Of that, but the Council could not expect , him when appealed to by his best clients to refuse to take service for them in a matter that would not affect the Corporation in the slightest until after his services as Town Clerk had terminated. The only tune when he could do anything on behalf of his clients would be when the matter went into Committee, which it could not do until after the Easter recess. So far as the question of the poll was concerned„it had not been his intention to do an atom on behalf of the gentlemen representing those works, but if the Council had the slightest doubt about it he said' that he would at once entirely retire from the service of the Town Council, or if there was the slightest doubt that he should be in the least degree influenced in anything he did in connection with the bill. In doing what he did he had regard to the fact that when he offered to resign he said that he was perfectly willing to conduct the bill through Parlia- ment. That offer was not accepted, and be therefore did not see why he should be prejudiced, after the .25th March, from accepting business which was important to him and his clients„and moreimportant to him froos the fact that if he had not taken it up his clients would have gone to other solicitors. If that xplanation was not satisfactory he should be sorry-, because he could give no other : and he thought he had better say at once that after the rem4lks of Coencillor Henry Roberts it would be advisable for his connection with the-Town Council to cease t once. The Moon : Does anyone- second Councillor Henry Robert's amendment?

Alderman Mirrox thought it was a very sore point,but inasmuch as that bill of costs would have to go before the General Purposes Committee, and would have to be taxed before it was paid, he did not see that the Council could be iri .'any worse position by passing it that evening_

Alderman CROSPIELD should like to know how it was that the expenses already connected with the Bill which was being promoted had reached. £l,OOO r £1,200. lie believed those were tho figures named by the Town Clerk.

The Torn; CLIME About £1,000; I think. Alderman CROSFIELD had always understood that an unooposod Bill would go through Parliament for about 000, and he did not understand how the expenses could already have reached such a sum as £l,OOO. As he understood it. the barristers who were engaged in con- nection with the Bill were not paid anything more than a fee of something like fire guineas to secure their sr- vices; and he could not see how £l,OOO had mounted up. He did not know whether the Council were that evening going to sanction the purchase of the Waterworks. Alderman FlAltnisoN : It has been done. Alderman IVRLORT : So far as we are concerned. ADDRESS BY THE REV. JOUR YONGE. The annual meetings of the Lancashire Congrega- tional Union have been held during the week at Blackburn. The Conference of the Union took place in the forenoon of Wednesday, in the Park-road Congregational Chapel. The Rev. John Yonge,af Warrington, Chairman of the Union, presided over a large attendance of delegates, both minieteral and. lay. _

The Chairman, in his annual address, referred' to the removal from among them of The late Rev.' Dr. Macfadyen, who he said was an able and eloquent preacher, a wisee inventive, and capable administra- tor, a diligent and faithful pastor, a kind, brotherly man, who fulfilled a ministry of high order with suce ce-s. The interest& of Congregationalism, esPeci- ally in Lancashire-, were dear to his heart, and received enthusiastic zervice. from his hand. No presence, he took it, was so largely mimed fr me their gattsering as that of De. Macfayden. They, could not but lament their loss, even while they found heart to re- joice in his gain, remembering that to him death was not Calamity but coronation: During the pest year, t°°e' death had removed thelleve.H. J. Johns. of Haslingden, H. H. Scullard, of Bolton,, and Thomas Peters, late of Widnes, and an eminent layman among Congregational- ists in the late Mr. J. G. 31•111innies. The Chairmary proceeded to speak on the subject of the Church's posi- tion in the present day. He held that it was a deeply significant fact of to-day that Christians of all deno-e minations were turning to the mission of the Christian Church. On all hands, indeed, without the Church as' well as within, the question was heine frequently asked, "What are churches for ?" He did not think the. reading of the Scriptures in public worship or preaching were made asi useful as they ought to be. He was afraid the Bible was one of the we:eat-read books of thee' day. Men were talking freely about the decline of th pulpit, and saying that its place was being taken up by the press. They as ministers were not jealous of the press, but they were jealous for the pulpit. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that the way to restore the power of the pulpit was to prove that it had a definite message for the new age, that it could adapt ,ifif to pressing needs and burning questions, and that, as of old, the spirit of the prophets existed. Then men would listen and would learn. Congregational churches were, in many cases, too confident in the oneanan ininistrjr. He believed they ought to have 'a far larger body of lay preachers in their churches than they had. (Applause.) It was difficult to induce their more intelligent and able laymen to take up this . work, and yet they wore not without the' capacity ef speeds. They coul " debate only too fluently in, Town Councils or at political meetings, and why cool", heyenot use their talents in the direct service 0' Christ and the Gospel ? Perhaps they were affected 'bY the unwiffiegness of many coneregations to have la). preachers, but their laymen needed to be encoura,ged preach, and then congregations needed to be trained tO listen to them (laughter), so that their ministers, in the name of the church, might have fuller opportunity tO Amrry the Gospel to those who stood without, and Nth° 'would not as yetcross the threshold of theirsanctuaries• They had tried to popularise services. They had catered for kinds of musicae taste, and had attempted all kieds of sensational talk. Special missions had bees ,reserted to, and probably by all those methods sense good had been done ; yet as a means of influencing the masses towards the churches and towards religion all these effort, had largely failed. The people in effect had 'saidrthey did not care for the churches because the churches did not care for them, but were sepremelY selfish: and entirely careless and indifferent as te their condition and circumstances. But Cengree gationalisra was exceptionally democratic. It believe(' in the people, it was meant fesr the people, and it err nottrue tesay that Congregationalism was meant on'Y for the middle classes. It was perfectably adaptable to all Classes. The higher classes might come to them, they must goto the lower. (Applause.) He urged uP°rl thoeepresentatives of their churches in this poeul°tl9 county the value and urgency of all movements that went to promote social Christianity. The conviction ripened and' spread that the churches of Christ most devise means.? dealing with the condition of what the Archbisliceeof Canterbury had described as "-suffering populations," and in the efforts to reach the people he did not overtook the work that might be done by women; It mighebe that a desirable method for the forwaru movement of the day was that of sisterhoods, such as- had already been established in connection with „ cen- tral London Wesleyan Mission. div.p: THE GYMNASTIC:COMPKIII- TION. WARRINGTON BEATS BOURNEMOUTH. .

The me-m—lier-s—O-Ithe Warrington Gymnasium gained another victory on Saturday, when they met a team from Bournemouth; in the second round of the competition for the 200 guinea challenge shield offered by the National Physical Recreation Society. Before entering into particulars of what proved to be s. very interesting contest, it may be stated that the Committee of the Warrington Gymnasium are _endeavouring to raise the sum of £455 towards the coat of erecting a suitable building for a public Fgymnasium and newspaper reading room. So popu- lar has the gymnasium become, that the room now Used for the exercises is found altogether inade- quate in size and accommodation, and, there being bo other room in the town available and suitable for the purposes of a gymnasium, the committee have to face the necessity of erecting a building, with the gxtUres and arrangements requisite for Such an Institution. The recent success of the local team in defeating the London team in the competition for the shield, which has once been won by Exeter Hall, is very satisfactory, looking to the fact that the gymnasium has only been established a little over twelve months. As has been previously stated, the Charity Commissioners are prepared to hand over a sum oi about .E6OO. (the proceeds of the sale of the former Workingmen's Club), towards the erection of the Institution; but the money is promised only on condition that the same classof persons are bene- fited as were intended to be benefited by the former Workingmen's Club, and that any further funds necessary to complete the building are forthcoming. Since then the committee have secured, from Lord Winmarleigh, a site in •a central position in the town, for the small sum of £2OO, which is much below its actual value. The committee estimate that the total cost of erecting a building, and fitting it up with the necessary appliances, including cost of site, will be about £1,:300; of this sum they have promised in subscriptions, including the amount 'Lora the Charity Commissioners, the sum of about 4-615, and the balance required is ..D155. The list of subscriptions is headed by Sir Gilbert Greenall, With £100; Messrs. F. Monks, T. Morris, and D. Jones have each promised £25; Messrs. H. Fergu- son, W. Pierpoint, W. Owen, and J. E. Wright each £10; and Messrs. R. Fairclough, J. Evans, J. Hes- heth, W. H. J. Jenkins, W. Dimelow, and J. L. Whittle, .£5 each. When the Warrington team lowered the colours of Exeter Hall—much to the surprise of the latter, it may be added—the popularity of the local combination received a very considerable filip. It was seen that there was a possibility of Warrington being somewhere ,ery close to victory at the finish of the contests, and the teault of the interest that has been taken in the subject since Warrington beat one of the crack competing teams wag seen in the densely crowded state of the Sankey-st. circus, where the competition with Bournemouth took Place, on Saturday evening. The building is a large one, but it was crammed before the proceedings commenced, and numbeis of people who had intended being present ha.d no alternative but to go away disappointed, the tuatrances having been closed soon after 'seven o'clock. Amongst those who were present were the Mayor (Alder- Irian Francomb), Alderman Sutton, Alderman Wright, 'Councillors Henry Roberts, Pierpoint, Fleming, Hutchin- son, and Muir, Hr. Peacocke, Messrs. W. Owen, Thomas Itiorris, J. Lyon Whittle, W. Reid, T. B. Kiernan, James Smethurst, E. J. Rose, C. J. Holmes, J. B. Dewhurst, H. I.Evans (hon. sec.), 3r.c. The teams, each consisting of eight athletes, were as under :—Bournemouth Mr. B. Minter (director), Messrs. F. Atkins, A. Barnes, H. M. Bond, A. Macklin, H. E. S. Monks' F. Stroud, and H. G. Riddett. War- rington ; Mr. E. Alexander (director), Messrs. A. Vernon, F. Turner, G. Vernon, W. H. Podmore, T. Locker, J. E. Warren, J. Holmes, and J. Podmore. The judges were the Her. E. 'r. Cross, of Bedford Leigh, and Mr. G. H. Barker of Liverpool. There were four contests included in the competition. The first was a combined display by each eight of single bar-bell exeecises, marks (maximum number 98) being allowed for precision, grace, and beneficial movements. The competitors were pretty evenly matched in this event, but Bournemouth took a slight lead with 90 marks, against 88 obtained by Warrington. The pianoforte accompaniments necessary to this exercise were ~.Played by Mrs. Hill (Bournemouth), and Mr. J. H. "right (Warrington). The second item was a voluntary exercise on the parallel bars, marks being awarded for the beet exhibition of strength, skill, agility, and grace. in these exercises, many of which were extremely difficult, the local men secured a lead which they ten tained throughout. Miles, for Bournemouth, made • marks out of a possible 12, and for Warrington, 2olmes made 11, A Vernon and Locker 9. F. Turner 9, W. H. Podmore 8, and J. Podmore 8. The aagrvgate figures were—Bournemouth, 44; Warrington, 4.w. This great advantage placed Warrington in a posi. On of comparative security,but the visitorswere plucky, gave an exhibition of jumping in the next portion of contest that was very creditable to them. They ,a Contest slot succeed in beating the Warrington men in this l'et'Pect, but they ran them a deal closer than many People expected. The first jump was 41t. 2in., and Fradually members of each team had to retire as the `ath was raised inch by inch. Turner cleared 4ft. 7in., it failed at the addition of another inch, and 'Warren and G.Vernen, of the local men, also had to retire. Atkins, Barnes, and Iliddett, of the Bournemouth team, Tetired at 41t. 9in., but J. Podmore, for Warrington' eared it, and was left last in. He cleared another inch, °ln failed at 4ft. llin. The total scores in this com- Petition were—Warrington 39, Bournemouth 37. A tiand-over-hand rope climbing contest was the last item, !rid in this Warrington finished 9k marks ahead. The result was a substantial victory for Warrington by marks, and the team now becomes entitled to enter 112 e semi-final for the shield, Sefton Hall being the team neY will have to meet. The other clubs remaining in Pe competition are Liverpool, and Dundee or Dublin. rules under which the shield is competed for provide , • at each member of the winning " eight" and their • str uctor shall receive a " Milton" Shield in ,reP"usse silver (valued at £25), and that the " eight" \and their Instructor) recording the second, highest aggregate number of marks (in the final) shall each receive a Shield in bronze, emblematic of "Fame," (trained at £5.) div.head: WEST HAM TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE WEST HAM TRAGEDY.

The inquest on the body of the girl Amelia Jeffs was resumed at West Ham, on Monday.—Mrs. Jeffs said her daughter knew no one employed on empty houses at Portman-road, but she had pointed out a caretaker to witness, saying, "There is old daddy watchman."— Samuel Roberts, watchman, was next called. Witness said he had never opened the door of the house in which the body was found.—Joseph Roborts, father of the care- taker, said the key of that particular house had been missing for five or six months, as also was the duplicate key.—TheCoroher rbmarked that, judging from all the circumstances, the girl went in by the front door, and the disappearance of the keys was an important point, which should be followed. He therefore adjourned the inquiry for a week.

WARRINGTON AMATEUR SAILING CLUB.

Sir,—Would you kindly permit me to ask through the columns of your valuable paper whether there exists, at the present time, such an institution as the above. There was one the season before last, but last year little or nothing of its movements was known; in fact I believe the annual race was abandoned. I should be sorry to hear of its falling through from want of stimulus on the part of either officers or members, but, as the yachting season is close upon us, surely some movements ought to be being made in tke way of calling meetings. Per- haps the Secretary or some other officer will reply, and oblige.—Yours truly,
A SUBSCRIBER.
FUNERALS IN INCLEMENT WEATHER.

Sir,—The fact of Mr. Gladstone's having caught a flsvero cold at Lord Sydney's funeral has once more drawn public attention to the risk attendant upon stand- Jig bireheaded at the graveside. It is impossible to estimate the number of deaths occasioned by this prac- tice, the danger of which has been pointed out again and again. The Church of England Funeral Reform Associ- ation, in a leaflet which has received the approval of four archbishops and thirty-five bishops, says :—" Mourners are not to do anything, or leave anything undone, im- perilling their own health, or that of the community." If this principle were observed, many lives would be saved. It would be a gain if the first part of the Burial Service were said in the church, which the deceased had been in the habit of attending, instead of in the Cemetery • Chapel. Neighbours and friends could then pay their last tribute of respect to the departed without attending the cemetery at all, thus avoiding exposure to the weather, and saving much valuable time.—Yours obediently,
F. LAWRENCE, Hon. Sec. Church of Enzland Funeral Reform Associ- ation. Viestow Vicarage, York, sth March, 1890.
"FACTS."

Sir,—" Samolitnede " is still writing his ungentle- manly letters; he is evidently not capable of viewing the religious events that are passing in this country, or he would not ask me to be silent. He would rather use his power (if he has any) to set forth the scriptures,when, by the proper use of his talents, he might be exposing evil, and convincing men of the infinite good to be found in the knowledge of Christ. To ask me to drop con- -troversy,one of the best methods of arriving at the truth, by exposing error, is as logical as saying Christ. John or Paul were not Christians, though their lives were full of it. On one occasion we read it continued daily for two years, resulting in both Jews and Greeks bearing the word; disputes daily in the market place at Athens. We read,too, of Paul withstanding Peter to the face for acting inconsistently; of Stephen disputing with the high priest and others. We are informed of Peter and John being brought up before the Rulers, Elders, and Scribes. Christ called the Pharisees and Scribes, hypocrites, fools, full of wickedness. He rebuked James and John and even told poor Peter he had a devil lam perfectly well aware that many people do not like truth, especially gospel truth, and no doubt this was why Paul was called a pestilent fellow. Lucian wrote, "He that will freely speak and write must be for ever no slave, under no prince or law, but lay out the matter truly as it is, not caring what any one will like or dislike." Bishop Jayne sets his face as did his predecessor against the Evangeli- cals, but fails to reprove men under him who hold Romish doctrines and belong to the E.C.U.,a society whose object is to bring the Church back again to bondage with Rome, reviles the Reformers and the Reformation, defies the Law, opposes the Bishops, contemns the laity and Non- conformists, and exalts the Priesthood into Sacrificing Priests, sympathises with the Jesuits, maintains ritual as the exponent of Doctrine, upholds the Confessional, as witnessed in a sermon lately at Worcester by Canon Knox Little in which he advised the newly ordained to confess to him, and then train their flocks to confess to them. Will our Vicar explain to his" dear people" why he selects two such men as Revds. Darwell and Cogswell? By their fruits they are known. Does Bishop; Jayne ever rebuke them that they may be sound in the faith ? Echo answers, never. Jude exhorts Us to earnestly contend for the faith.

div.head: ROBERT FOULKES.
div.p: ROBERT FOULKES.
Frodsham, Feb. 25. 1890. THE ANNUAL ACCOUNTS OF PUBLIC CHARITIES.

Sir,—A short time ago I read a paper on "The Public Charities of the Northwich Division" in which I stated that those persons having their control or management were required by law to render annually a statement of their receipts and expenditurelto the ratepayers at the annual township vestry meeting. Since then I have received so many enquiries respecting the above state- ment that I venture to ask you to allow me the use of your columns in order that I may quote the section of the Act I then referred to, the more so as the question of the administration of Public Charities is of wider importance than the boundaries of the Northwick Divisipn, and the fact that within the next few weeks, the annual township vestry meetings throughout the Oountry will be held. The Charitable Trusts Act 1855, 18 and 19 Vict., Cap. 24, sec. 44, enacts that " Trustees of all charities shall send annual statements of their accounts to the Charity Commissioners, made up to the 31st day of December in every year, on or before the 25th day of March follow- ing, and in the case of parochial charities the trustees shall deliver another copy thereof to the churchwarden or churchwardens of the parish or parishes with which the objects of such charities are identified, wins shall present the same at the next general meeting of the vestry of such parishes and insert a copy thereof in the minutes of the vestry book, and every such copy shall be open to the inspection of all persons at all reasonable hours, subject to such regulations as to the said board nay seem fit; and any person may require a copy of every such account or of any part thereof after the rate of twopence for every seventy-five words or figures." The Public Charities of the Count v of Cheshire produce an annual income approaching L 2-0,000, and the above means of keeping in memory their existence and their , annual expenditure should be remembered at every I annual vestry meeting. If, as I believe, their not being i reported and entered in the township vestry minute hooks has been due to imperfect knowledge of the statutory obligation, it is to be hoped these accounts will in future be regularly submitted; and, where they are net so, that some person will at once ask for their production, and if need be, move the adjeurnment of the meeting in order to give further opportunity for their being so pro- duced.

The Charity Commissioners, in one of their annual reports, remarks "the obligation to make such returns and a liability to have the obligation enforced, at all times induces accuracy on the part of the adminstrators of charities in the discharge of the duties. It is import- ant that all persons interested in endowments should be able to exercise their right of examining such accounts of their management."—Very faithfully yours. WM. HANDLEY. Runcorn, March sth, 1890.

div.head: PURCHASE OF THE WARRINGTON WATER-
div.p: THE PURCHASE OF THE WARRINGTON WATER-
WORKS.
Sir,—The enclosed correspondence may prove interest- ing to your readers. (con.)

February 28th, 890. To the Town Clerk, Warring- ton. Dear Sir,—l journeyed to the ratepayers' meeting last Friday evening, for the purpose of asking the following questions, but had to leave before an opportunity oc- curred for me to do so. If you will answer them it will save the time of the meeting next Monday. What rating powers do the Corporation take under the proposed Act of Parliament? What is the maximum rate per £ the ratepayers will be liable to? Will the rate for the pur- chase of the Waterworks be levied on all property rated to the poor, whether the occupier does or does not use the water? What reasons do the Council give to the ratepayers to show them that the sources of the supply af the company are sufficient in quantity, and suitable JIII quality, not only for the present but in the future, and

that such sources will not in the future become contam- inated by increase of population in the surrounding dis- tricts, or in the district itself, from which the water is obtained, or the supply diminished in quantity from causes over which the Company's Act gives them no con- trol, viz. i—sinking of wells outside the district named in the Act, and the various other natural laws to which all water supply obtained by pumping is liable. Why Miould the loan debt of the company be added to the capitalised amount of purchase, the basis of purchase being the money earned partially by the loan capital ? Is the authority to use present surplus revenue to increase former dividends to the maximum rate derived from the Company's Act, or from what other Act ? I shall feel obliged by you letting me have the information at your earliest convenience.—Yours,

div.head: T. Gnaavra. 30, South-road, Waterloo, near Liverpool, March 6th, 1890. e
div.p: T. Gnaavra. 30, South-road, Waterloo, near Liverpool, March 6th, 1890. e
Town Clerk's Office, Warrington, Ist March, 1890.

Dear Sir. Purchase of Waterworks.—The only answer I can give to your letter of the 28th ult., is that if the Corporatibn purchase this undertaking they will step in- to the shoes of the Company so far as regards the charges for the supply of water, and in the event of any deficit It will be charged upon the borough rate.—Yours truly, W. H. BROOK. Mr. T. Greaves, 30, South-rd.. Waterloo, Liverpool.

I hope some member of the Council will be good enough to answer the questions I addressed to the Town Clerk, for my information and that of my fellow rate- payers. It appears a farce for the Mayor to call a meeting ot the ratepayers, to sanction the cost of promoting a bill in Parliament, when the press informs us that the said bill was read a second time on March 4th. The coqts we are asked to sanction have evidently been already incurred without our sanction.—Yours, &c.,__

div.head: T. oREAVES.
div.p: T. oREAVES.
THE POLL-A SUGGESTION.

Sir,—l suppose that, after the town's meeting on Mon- day evening, a poll of the ratepayers of Warrington will be taken. At the meeting the Mayor stated that it was a legal necessity for the meeting to accept or reject the bill as a whole, and that no official vote could be taken as to any particular part of the bill. It would be inter- esting to know if the same ruling applies to the poll. For my own part I should have no hesitation in approv- ing the whole bill, as I think it a thoroughly useful measure, but, as is very well known, there are a large number of ratepayers who strongly object to certain parts, and lam af raid if it is put en bloc it will be lost. Would it not be b•tter for those who are engineering the bill to disarm hostility as far as possible by making it thoroughly well known, before the poll takes place, that they intend to drop or modify what they know to be the most unpopular clauses.—Yours, &c., .
: A VOTER.

div.head: LORD CROSS AND THE INDIAN FACTORY 'ACTS.
div.p: LORD CROSS AND THE INDIAN FACTORY 'ACTS.

At the Blackburn and District Ch4mber of Com- merce. on Tuesday, the following letter was read from Lord Cross, the Secretary of State for India "I am directed by the Secretary of btate for India in Council, to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, dated the 16th February, conveying the views of the Blackburn Chamber of Commerce on the Indian Factory Bill, the heads of which have been telegraphed from Calcutta to the "Times" newspaper. When the Bill, which has been laid before the Indian Legislature, reaches Viscount Cross, the remarks of the Uhamber will be care- fully considered by his lordship in Council. It will, doubtless, be in yotir recollection, that the prin- ciples on which the Indian Factory Acts were to be amended were fully set out in the papers presented to the House of Commons (No. 162), and ordered to be printed on the 23rd May. 1889.-1 am, sir, your obedient servant. A. GODLEY. The President of the Incorporated Chamber of Commerce, Black- burn."

div.head: – – A RUNCORN PUBLICAN HEAVILY
div.p: - - A RUNCORN PUBLICAN HEAVILY

FINED. Before Mr. Jos. Reynolds and Mr. Jas. Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph AV, landlord of the Old Bridgewater Arms, Percival's-. Fine, was summoned for having. on the 22nd February,unlawfully permitted drunkenness to take place on his premises; and also with permitting his premises to be the habitual resort, or place of meeting of pmstitutes, the latter having been allowed to remain therein fir a longer period than was necessary for reasonable refreshment.—Jessie Wood and Louisa Spen- cer, Women of ill-fame, were charged with being drunk in the Bridgewater Arms, on the 22nd February, anti pleaded guilty.—P.S. Woolley stated that on the Satur- day nigh, in question, about half-past nine, he visited the Old Bridgewater Arms, and in the vault he found the two women. Wood had a glass of gin before her, and Spencer had a glass of whisky. Both women were drut.k. Witness left the house, and waited in the road for nearly half-an-hour, when he returned and found the women still in the same place. He asked Mrs. Abel where her husband was, and she replied, " He is inside, but he cannot be seen; he is drunk in bed." He told her she had got prostitutes in the house, and she said "Yea, I know. Will you wait while I turn them out." He remained, and she ordered them out. On the first of February, he cautioned Mr. Abel about this thing occur- ring on his premises, and he said he would see that the women did not go there again. He had continually se• n these women on the premises.—By Mr. A. Linaker (who defended Mr. Abel) : He did not know that they had had a great deal of trouble with prostitutes at the Old Bridgewater Arms. They had frequented the neighbour- hood since Abel commenced to sell them drink, or else they did not use to.—Mr. Linaker pleaded guilty to the summonses and addressed the Bench in mitigktion of penalty. These women entered the house, and were served as a matter of right hut they would linger beyond a reasonable time, and they had been frequently ordered out, and forcibly ejected. On the night in question, Mrs. Abel ordered Wood and Spencer out of the house time after time. He admitted that technical offence had been committed in not haying sent for the police to put them out—lnspector Bowyer said Abel was cautioned only that very day abreit harbouring prostitutes—Mrs. Abel was called and corroborated their advocate's statement, and said that she had frequently refused to serve the woman.—Spencer: Never.—ln reply to the Inspector, witness said her husband was in the kitchen when the policeman entered the house.—Mr. Reynolds said there must be some cause for the prostitutes as- sembling in that house—Mr. Linaker said the house they used to frequent, the Blue Ball, in Fryer-st., was now closed, and the women were distributed amongst other publicaes, who had a great deal to contend with. —Mr. Reynolds: That has been closed for 18 months.— Mr. Linaker said the publicans could not refuse the women refreshments.—The Inspector: They won't go to places where they won't have them. This has been going on since last November. Mr., Reynolds said it was quite evident that the house was the resort of prostitutes, and if they did not know they were going to he treated very leniently in the house, they would not visit it so much as they had done. The magistrates had decided tofine Abel £2. nd costs 9s. 111., for permitting drunkenness; or in default, one month. For harbouring prostitutes,he would be fined £5 and met* 9s. ed. : or in default two months imprisonment. Had not this been the first offence, his license would have been endorsed.—Wood and Spencer were each tined 10s. and costs, or 14 d tys' imprisonment.
