That the first annual concert and soiree of Run- corn Liberal Club, on Monday evening next, is expected to he a great success. That Mr. Brunner has resumed his Parliamentary duties, and will be unable to attend the soiree for the very satisfactory reason that the division on the Commission Report is expected to take place on that night, and his vote will be required. , That in accordance with his declaration during the recent Runcorn School Board election, Mr. flowitt introduced the subject of free education at the meeting of the Board on, Tuesday evening, and made a motion in favour of such a system of , National education. •

That in face of the recent discussion in Parliament, Mr. Howitt did not elaborate his views, but argued on the broad princirle that what was compulsory should also be free; and Mr. Taylor, ia seconding the proposition, showed how the present system of fees oppressed poor parents. That Dr. Gastaldi unburdened himself of a most eloquent oration, of which the kernel was, that he did not object to Free Education, if the manage- ment of voluntary schools was retained in its pre- sent form, and religious teaching permitted. That the Vicar,while not approving or ,li.sentiug, proposed an amendment evading the poi.i at issue.' In a long speech be set forth the diffien'ties sur- rounding the subject, and submitted an elaborate calculation showing that if Free Education were to be paid out of the rates, what a terrible increase there would be in the same.

That it seems to be forgotten that the State now contributps about three fourths of the cost of Ele- mentary Education, and surely it cannot be such a great step for the State to provide the remaining fourth and abolish school fees.

That each member of the Board spoke on the subject, and, with the exception of the Vicar, they observed the long established custom of rising when addressing the chair. -Is the Vicar seeking to bring about a" reform" in this matter, or is he, as a new member, unaware of the courteous custom, or does he consider the Vice Chairman above the rule?

That the upholders of Mr. Higginson, surveyor to the Widnes Local Board, have by their agitation secured that his claims to be re-elected to the post shall be considered along with the claims of the selected candidates of the 169 who have applied. That at the ratepayers' meeting on Friday night, Mr. Randall made some charges with respect to cer- tain contracts, which ought not to rest where they are. In these matters a Local Board ought, like Cmsar's wife, to be above suspicion.

div.head: EXMIINER, SATURDA Y, MATCH 8. 1890.
div.p: THE EXMIINER, SATURDA Y, MATCH 8. 1890.
A DOMESTIC SERVANT AND HER OUTFIT.

Mary Emma Rushton, of 8, Hutchinson-street, was brought up at Widnes Court, on Monday; charged %ith stealing three dozen brass rings, one brush, and a purse, valued at 45., from a ahoy in Waterloo-road, Widnes, on the 28th ult., the pro- perty of William 'Wray. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—lnspentor Keighley said, on Friday after- noon, the 28th ult., the prisoner went into the shop of Mr. Wray, smallware dealer, in Waterloo-road, and after she had left a box of lings and the brush produced was I missed. The prisoner was further charged with stealing, a pair of trousers, valued at 6s. lid., from the pawn- shop of Mr. C. R. Neil, Albert-road, Widnes, on the 21st I ult.—lnspector Keighley said that about five o'clock on I the afternoon of the 21st ult., the prisoner asked a little girl named Williams to go with her up Albert-road. She went into Mr. Neil's pawnshop, and on coming out gave the pair of trousers to the girl Williams. and told her to pledge them at Jameson's pawnshop, in Ann-street. Four and sixpence was lent on them to the girl Williams, who on giving the money to the prisoner received a penny for having pledged them.—The prisoner pleaded guilty on both charges, and said she stole the goods to enable her to go to service.—lnspector Keighley said the prisoner was before the Court in December last, for stealing a pair of boots, but was discharged.—The Ber,ch imposed a fine of L 1 in each case, or in default of payment one month's imprisonment. •

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE MR. SAMUEL WHITE OF RUNCORN.
div.p: WILL OF THE LATE MR. SAMUEL WHITE OF RUNCORN.

Probate of the will, bearing date 25th November 1889, of the late Mr. Salim] White; of Oreenway- rd., Runcorn, with two codicils annexed has been granted the executors, Mr. James Kirkham, builder, of Runcorn, Mr. John Frodsham, public accountant, Runcorn, and the grand-daughter of the deceased, Sarah Ann Thompson. The gross value of the estate is sworn under £27,139 9s. 3d. The deceased be- queaths to his wife Mary, for life, his freehold house in Greenway-rd., together with the furniture therein, and the sum of 30s, per week; after her decease the said house and furniture is bequeathed to his granddaughter Edith Thompson, absolutely. After directing the execu- tors to expend £l.OO in purchasing furniture for his two granddaughters, Edith and Sarah Ann Thompson, ha further directs the executors to rent a house for their use. A legacy of £lOO is bequeathed to the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, and bequests of £lO are made to several relations. Other relatives are each bequeathed £2O. The execu- tors are then to stand possessed of the sum of £5,000 and invest the same "as therein mentioned " and to pay the income thereof to his granddaughter Edith Thompson, during her life ; and a further sum of £5,000 to pay the income tkereof to his granddaughter Sarah Ann Thompson for her life; and on their decease,to the children if any of the said Edith and Sarah Ann Thompson in equal shares. The income of £2,500 has to be paid to his grandson Samuel Thompson during his life, and in case of death leaving issue to his children in equal shares absolutely. Provision is also made as to the residue of the estate. The will was extracted by Messrs. Davies, Sharp, Kir- connell and Co., Warrington.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of this Board was held on Monday afternoon, for tho purpose of receiving and considering the applications for the vacant surveyor- ship to the Board and other business. Mr. F. H. Gossage, IP., presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Handley, _Wright, 11. Titninis, S. Sadler' Houghton, H. Haskell, jun., Taylor. Reyes, Cook, Slid wood, and Allen (clerk). THE VACANT SURVETORSIIIP. The Chairman stated that he had received a petition asking him to call a public meeting of the ratepayers to consider the action of the Board with reference to the resignation of Mr. lligginson, the surveyor, and as he was away from home, defore he could deal with it, the promoters had decided to call a meeting on their own account.

The resolutions passed at the ratepayer's meeting, on Friday, were now read, and the Chairman said the Board could do nothing further than place Mr. Higginson's name amongst the selected candidates, and if the mem- bers wished to re-elect him they would thus have an opportunity of doing so.—Dr. O'Keeffe said he considered that Mr. Iligginson had vindicated himself sufficiently in the eyes of the public, and it would be a graceful act on the part of the Board to re-instate him in the position he had held with great benefit to the public for so many years. He contended that it was the wish of the rate- payers that Mr. Higginson should be re-elected, and their opinions ought not to be disregarded.—The Clerk in answer to the Chairman, ruled that it would be out of order to discuss this matter in that form, but Dr. O'Keeffe could if ho wished, propose the appointment of Mr. Higginson on his application.—Mr. Taylor said the Board had passed a strong vote of censure on Mr. Hig- ginson, and he should like to ask Dr. O'Keeffe if he had improved any in the meantime. There was no. under- hand work on the part of the Highway Committee on the matter, and he should like to ask where or when they had taken advantage of Mr. Higginson, in any shape or form. He did not see how the Board could !.ake Mr. ffig- ginson on again. Twelve months last July a vote of censure was passed on him, and he was no better now than he was then ; if anything he was worse.—Mr. Sadler said it had been notorious to everyone that the surveyor had not been performing his duties properly.—After further discuss;on, Dr. O'Keeffe agreed to the suggestion that Mr. Hig,ginson's name should be left amongst those gelected.—On the proposition of Mr. Cook, seconded by Mr. Gasket), it was resolved that the Chairmen of the respective Committees, with the Chairman of the Board, be a Committee to consider the applications, and tint six be selected to attend the meeting of the Board for elec- tion. The Committee therefore consists of Messrs. F. H. ' Gossage, H. Gaslcell, E. Carey, T. Handley, and S. Sadler.

THE PROPOSED FIRE STATION AND COTTAGES. The Clerk asked if the Board would give Mr. She!mei.- dine" some idea of what they intended to do with tegard to the new cottages and fire station tri be built in Lacey-st. Ile said there would be about 14 houses, wi h a frontage of 161 t. with a fire station in the centre. He produced plans, which had been considered by the Committee interested.—The estimated expenditure was about £2740. —Mr. Gaskell moved that the houses and fire station be provided. The Gas and Water Committee considered them necessary for the proper carrying on of the worle, and as the price wa.s a reasonable one, he thought the work should be done.—Mr. Cook seconded the resolution which was carried.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW MAIN ROAD.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW MAIN ROAD.

The Clerk submitted particulars from the Childwall Highway Board respecting the making of a main road between Widnes and Liverpool, starting from Ditton-road and running through the Townships of Ditton. Halewood, Much Wootton, Allerton, and Wavertree, a total length of 8 miles and 1012 yards. The Clerk also submitted another route running from Stewards' Brook through the townships of Ditton, Tarbuck, Little Wootton, and Child- wall to Liverpool, a distance of 7 miles and 1,300 yards which was more favourably received and subsequently adopted on the proposal of Mr. Taylor seconded by Mr. Cook.

div.head: DEACON-ROAD IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: DEACON-ROAD IMPROVEMENTS.

The Clerk laid upon the table plans, which had been forwarded, for the erection of a number of houses in Deacon-road, and for the laying out of some streets in connection therewith. According to an old plan ap- proved by the Board in 1876, Deacon-road was to be raised up to Appleton Quarry, to be on a leel with Frederick-st., when the latter extended so far. The Highway Committee could not approve of the plans now sent in, and it was necessary for the Board to say whether they would carry out the old plans, or whether they would formulate another plan. If it were decided to carry out the 1876 plan, a portion of the quarry would have to be pnrchased, so .that the approach to Appleton village could be widened. If the quarry was purchased, it would cost the Board ' between £5,000 and £6,000, which meant a penny in tbe pound on the rates for 20 or 30 years.—Mr. Taylor said the Highway Com- mittee were not prepared at present to carry out the scheme and purchase the quarry.—The Surveyor was Instructed to prepare plans to slightly raise Deacon-road to the level of Frederick-st., so as not to interfere with the original scheme.—The meeting then eonchzded.
RATEPAYERS' PROTEST AGAINST MR.. IGGIN- SON'S DISMISSAL.

Last night week a meeting of the ratepayers of Widnes', called by placard, was held in the Drill Hall or the purpose of protesting against the dis- missal of Mr. Thomas Higginson from his position •of eprveyorto the Widnes Local Board " afterfifteen years of good service" About 300 persons were present, and Mr. Valentine, of Halton View, was voted to the chair, and in his , opening speech dwelt upon the competency of Mr. Higginson, whom be described as a thorough ratepayers' man and one who went in for the benefit of the town. (Applause.) A Figs vey or , he said, must of the necessities" of his position have a certain amount of power, because he could not always be calling his committee together, and because he had used his power and his common sense,.helad met with the ,ffispleasures of his masters and after 15 of the beat years of his life had been spent in the service of the town, whose roads he had made the envy of the sur- rounding district, he was turned adrift. (Applause.)— Mr. D. Wright moved the first resolution, that the duties of the surveyor's department had been such, as required additional assistance, which ,although applied for,, was not accorded to him, and described Mr. Higginson as an honest man,whom no one could accuse of having accepted a bribe from any contractor; he was nobody's servantbut his employers'.—Mr. Hemingway seconded the motion which was carried unanimously.—A second resolution was moved by Mr. Randall (contractor), who stated that Mr. Higginson had honestly performed his duties,, and the work under his supervision had been substantially carried out.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved a third resolution stating that the fact that the roads in Widnes were main- tained at a less cost than in 200 other townships reflected credit upon Mr. Higginson.—Mr. Beech proposed that the inability of the surveyor to supply the committees with full details respecting work performed was due to his application for assistance not having been complied with.—Mr. W. J. Hargreaves moved the fifth and last resolution respectfully requesting the Local Board to take into consideration Mr. Higginson's long and arduous service, his acknowledged competency and courtesy,and to re-instate him in his office as surveyor of the Local Board. All these resolutions were unanimously carried.

div.head: LATE MR. MCMINNIES.
div.p: THE LATE MR. MCMINNIES.

At a recent meeting of the Cobden Club, an expression of the sincere regret of the Committee on the death of Mr. John Gordon McM innies, and of their recognition of his valuable services to the club as a member of the Committee, was ordered to be placed on the minutes. The Rev. John Yonge in his address, as chairman of the Congregational Union, at Blackburn, on Wednesday, referred to the great loss which Con- gregationalism had sustained by the death of Mr. McMinnie&

div.head: NOTABLE WEDDING. '
div.p: A NOTABLE WEDDING. '

It is not often that the combined ages of bride and bridegroom total up to more then 150 years, but this was the case with regard to a couple who entered into the bonds of wedlock at Great Sankey Church,on Monday. The bride was Mrs. Plinston, who used to be a farnilar figure in War- rington market.where she had a greengrocer's stallc and the bridegroom Mr. John Butterworth, who. recently returned from America and has lived in Latchford. Mrs. Plinston has more than completed her seventieth year,while Mr. Butterworth is in his 81st year. The Vicar of Great Sankey, the Rev. E. S. Jackson, officiated at the wedding, and after, wards the wedding breakfast was partaken of at the residence of the bride's grand-daughter, the Travellers' Arms, Dial-st., Warrington.

The Bank rate of discount was reduced on Thursday from sto 4 per cent. Damage to the amount of 300,000d01s was c.used by a fire which broke out on Wednesday in the dry-goods quarter of New York. Sentence of twelve months' hard labour was passed at the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday, on George Richards, a reporter, found guilty of abducting Emily Mary Riches, a young girl, Hying at West Ham. On Wednesday morning the steamer Nautilus, owned by the General Steam Navigation Company, sank at her moorings in the Thames from some cause which has not yet been ascertained. The Salford Town Council decided on Wednesday to petition Parliament for the appointment of a Royal Commission to hold a thorough inquiry into the late gas frauds in the borough. Great excitement prevails among the white settlers of Oklahoma in consequence of rumoured projects for col- onising the territory as a negro district. Some outrages have already been committed. _

The Queen held the first Drawing Room a the season, on Wednesday, at Buckingham Palace. The Duchess of Fife was presented by her mother. Altogether there were about a hundred presentations. Mr, John Catterall, an old and highly respected Pres- ton soliritor.died on Thursday morning at his residence at Lea, it is believed from grief—caused by the death of his son Louis on Saturday last, after two days illness, of influenza.

John Sandilands writes to Friday's "Glasgow Mail" contradictin,g Corporal Palmer's statement in the " Nine- teentleCentury " that two Glasgow Irishmen were shot as traitors during the battle of Te1.4.11-Kebir. Sandilands was in Rthrier's regiment, and says only two Glasgow men were killed by the enemy—Paterson and Pollock. A second edition "Times" telegram from Durban en Thursday confirms the reports of the rough reception of -Presidatt Kruger at Johannesburg, which is said to be the result of •discontent of the people with the failure of the Government to fulfil its promises. div.head: LocK-our IN. THE STEEL TRADE.
div.p: LocK-our IN. THE STEEL TRADE.

At Workington, on Friday, 800 men employed in the Bessemer department of Catnmell's Derwent Steel Works were locked out in consequence at a dispute respecting ten per cent. advance. There was considerable excite- ment.

ANOTHER PASSENGER TRAIN IN COLLISION. The 7.20 train from Stoke to Stafford, on Thursday, nig,ht came intocollision at a junction near Trentham with a goods train. The driver of the passenger engine was severely hurt, and the passengers shaken. Much damage was d(me. IMPENDING STRIKE OF ENGINEERS. A conference of masters and men in the engineering trade of the North of England was held at Newcastle yesterday afternoon. The former declined to reduce the hours by one hour a week, but offered a shilling increase per week in wages. This the men declined to accept, and 30,000, will leave work to-day.

A BODY UNEAIMIED BY DOGS. A shocking discovery has been made in St. Michael's Churchyard, Workington. The gravedigger, noticina two dogs scratching up ground furiously, drove them off. and found that they had unearthed a box containing the the body of a child. The head of the child was bent into its neck, and its knees were doubled up so as to enable it to be squeezed into the box. The police are investigating the matter.

div.head: STAMFORD ELECTION. , THE POLLING.
div.p: THE STAMFORD ELECTION. , THE POLLING.

Polling commenced yesterday morning in the Stamford division of Lincolnshire for the election of a member of Parliament in room Mr. J. C. Lawrance (Conservative), who has been made a judge. The candidates were Mr. Henry John Cockayne Cust (Conservative) and Mr. Arthur Priestly (Gladstonian Liberal). The principal centres of activity in the division are Grantham, Stamford, Bourne, and Corby, and the votes will be counted and the result declared at Bourne to-day (Saturday).

THE ALLEGED MURDER CONSPIRACY. TORONTO, FRIDAV.
The man Borchelt and his wife, who were a'rrested on suspicion of having been concerned in the murder a a young Englishman named Benwill. were remanded for seven days at Niagara Falls yesterday.

RAILWAY COLLISION IN AMERICA. SEVEN PERSONS KILLED. NEW YORK, FRIDAY. A terrible collision occurred yesterday to the Lake Shore passenger train from Chicago,yust to the west oi Buffalo. Seven persons were killed in the collision, and many re- ceived injuries.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—FRIDAr. The House met at three o'clock.

SCOTCH EDUCATION. Lord Nourom moved for a return relating to Scotch education but it was opposed and subsequently withdrawn. A NEW SPEAKER SNUFFED OUT. Lord TEYNRAII. addressing the House on a question not on tke paper, was called to order by Lord Faversham. Lord Teynham appealed to the Prime Minister to hear him. Lord SALISBURY said he would willingly listen tn him, but could not undertake to answer his question. Earl Granville instructed the noble lord who has not been long in the House, how to proceed, but Lord Teynham, persisting to addressthe ilouse,Lord CA4PYRDOWN moved that the noble lord be not heard. The motion was agreed to and the House adjourned,

div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS,

M'Canhy, said his atten- tion had been called ..to an article in the "Nineteenth Century" for the current month, entitled " A Rattle Described from the Ranks" by Arthur V. Palmer, "in which the author alleged the treacherous conduct on the part of two Glasgow Irishmen, at the battle of Tel-el- liebir." lie was sorry, however, be couldthrow,nnlight on the subject. Probably Sir Edward Hartley who took a distinguished part in the campaign wouNI be able to say something in the matter. . RETURN OP MR. LABOUCHERE.

Mr. Labehere entered the House during the tine Tn. James Ferguson WAS answering a questi.m, and the bon. gentleman was greeted with Nationalist cheers as he took a seat on the front bench below the gangway, norxt to Mr. Diliwyn.

div.head: TEE PARNELL, RRPORT.-A TORY DECLARES RM. MIND.
div.p: TEE PARNELL, RRPORT.-A TORY DECLARES RM. MIND.

Mr. JENNING9 said that in the event of the motion of the First Lord of the Treasury becoming a substantive resolution, he would move the addition of the following words "This House deems it its duty to record itecon- demnation of the conduct of those who are responsible for the accusation of complicity in murder brought against members ef this Howe discovered to be based mainly on forged letters and declared by the Special Commission to be disproved." (Loud Opposition cheers.).

div.head: T. PANCRAS VICTORY.
div.p: THE T. PANCRAS VICTORY.
' Mr. T. E. Bolton on taking the oath and his seatfor, St. Pancras was greeted with loud cheers.
IR OCADSTONE'S NOTION.

Mr. SDIIITff replying to Mr. Morley, said the votes in supply for the army and navy must be obtained before the Government could consider the question of giving a day for the consideration of Mr. Gladstone's motion arising out of Mr. Labouchere's sus- pension.

div.head: SPECIAL COMDTISSMN DEBATE.
div.p: SPECIAL COMDTISSMN DEBATE.

The debate on Mr. Gladstone's amendment respecting the Special Commission report, was then resumed by Mr. Justin McCarthy, who. rejoiced in the notice of motion just given by Mr. Jennings, which showed that at least one fair-minded gentleman sat on benches opposite. (Cheers.) Sir Henry James followed He found fault with the amendment of Mr. Gladstone as it took a, middle course; and he disliked the motion of Government betause it took no notice of some of the findings of the Commissioners. Mr. Asetorni thought the speech of the Attorney-General last night would live in the forensic annals of this country as a classic instance, of a shabby and ungenerous apology The House was counted out at a quarter to nine.

WHEREAS A PUBLIC MEETING of the Owners and Rate- payers of the Borough of Warrington was duly held on Friday, the 21st day of February, 1890; in the Public Hall, Rylands-street, and continued by adjournment on Monday, the 3rd day of March, 1890, at the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-st. in the said Borough, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 36th Victoria. cap. 91, intituled " An Act to authorise the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in certain cases." AND WHEREAS at the said Meeting held at the time and place aforesaid, I, as Chairman of such Meeting, and in corn_ pliance with the Statute, proposed the following Resolution THAT this Meeting, as representing the Owners and Rate- payers of the Borough of Warrington, do, pursuant to the provisions of the Act of the 35th and 36th Victoria,chapter 91, intituled " An Act to authorise the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in certain cases," approve of and consent to the following Resolutions of the Council of the said Borough, passed at their Meeting held in the Town Hall, Warrington, on the 19th day of December, 1889, namely ; " That the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough "of Warrington, acting by the Council do and they are " hereby empowered to apply to Parliament in the session of 1890, for a Bill intituled ' A Bill to extend the "boundaries of the Borough of Warrington, to proyide for "vesting the undertaking of the Warrington Watsrworks " Company in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of " of the Borough of Warrington. aud to make better pro- vision for the health, local government, and improve- ment of the Borough, and for other purposes.' ' " That the costs, charges, and expenses, preliminary and incidental to the applying for promoting and passing such Bill into an Act, shall be charged upon the Borough Fund and Borough Rate." , AND WHEREAS the said Resolution, on being put, was not carried, whereupon demand was made that such question should be decided by a Poll of Owners and Ratepayers. : NOW THEREFORE I hereby give notice as follows :- 1. That such Poll will, as by law required. be taken under the provisions of Hy! Public Health Act, 1875, by means of 1 Voting Papers. 2. TIIAT I shall cause one of such Voting Papers to be delivered by persons appointed by me for that purpose at the address within the Borough stated in the claim of each , Owner or Proxy, and at the residence within the Borough of each Ratepayer entitled to vote therein, on Wednesday, the 126th day of March, 1890. Any person entitled to receive a Voting paper who shall not receive such Voting Paper on 1 that day, will, on personal application to me. at the Town Clerk's Office, Town Hall, on any day before Monday. the 31st day of March, 1890, be entitled to receive a Voting Paper from me, and to fill up the same in my presence, and then and there to deliver the same to me. 3. THAT such Voting Papers will be called for and collected by the persons appointed by one for that purpose, on Monday, the 31st day of March. IS9O, between tile hours of Eight in the Forenoon and Seven in the Afternoon. 4. THAT the Votes given on such Poll will be examined and cast up at the Town Hall, in the said Borough, on Tues- s , ay, the let day of April. 1890, and on as many days imme- ' 'ately succeeding as may be necessary ; and that if any Oting Paper, duly delivered, shall not have been collected through my default, or that of the persons appointed to collect the same, the Voter in person may deliver the same to me at the Town Hall before Twelve o'clock at noon on the said Ist day of April, 1890. AND I hereby further give notice that any Owner or Proxy will he entitled to have a Voting Paper delivered to him, if, on or before Tuesday, the 11th day of March, 1890. he sends a claim in writing to me, at the Town Clerk's Office. Lyme Street. containing the particulars required by the Second Schedule to the Public Health Act, 1875, to be co:stained in claims. AND further, that forms of claim may be obtained on personal application at the Town Clerk's Office, Lyme Street. DATED this 4th day of March, 1890. RICHARD WALKER FRANCOMB, Mayor.

"Oh yes, of course," said Martin, sneeringly. "Now you are going to preach, and improve the occasion, I suppose. There, for goodness sake, Mark, don't be such a prig." "How much money co you owe this—this ma- r said Mark, looking with an expression of disguyt the ugly features of the follow where he lay, with the light from a lamp shining full upon him. "What's that to you!" said Martin, sulkily. "Only this much, that if you will let this affair be a warning to you, and give me your word that you will leave all there sporting associates and devote yourself to your work. I will pay the debt—if I can." "Do you mean that, alarTs ?" cried Marta* "Yes, I mean it—if you are to be trusted." "All right then, I will, old feltow—l will be trusted. I'm sick of it all. I only owe that blackguard twentf pounds, and he came hutting me at the office for ii this afternoon." "I know he did," said Mark, quietly. "And does old Klop know it?" "It was Mr. Klopstock, your best friend, who told "lla, ha! That's good," said Martin, with a forced laugh. "My best friend! Why, the old boy hat' me.' "And yet be has kept you on when another, for • tithe of your offences, would have bren ignominiously disnissea." 'Yes. All right. I know. But look here, Mark, you'll pay this twenty, won't you?" "What was the debt for?" "Well," said Martin, sulkily; "it was a bit of het; but if you're going to cross-examine a fellc I' a just as lief you did not pay." "I'm neither going to preach nor cross examine. Martin," said his brother. "Give me your word that, to-night's escape shall be the turning point in sOur folly, and I will pay this man. More, let me see that you are truly sorry, and try to make up for the lost past* and, as far as I can, I will pay all your debts. Can brother say fairer than that?' " No, no, of course not. You are a regular brick. Mark, and I will drop all the betting. How shiver, I am! There, I'm dressed now. Let's get away from this 'floating den. I seem to smell the muddy water now." Worrall still slept soundly, and upon the servant on duty being appealed to, he was content to tske- their names and addresses. " We'll, wait upon you, sir, if our friend thert. wants a summons against you for attempted murder." "Bah r said Martin, contemptuously. "Migbt just as wellcharge him." " SO I suppose, sir, or I shouldn't be so easy ; and after a few more preliminaries the brothers weall ashore, and Martin preferred walking to a ride borne; but he let his brother carry the bag, heavy with bi° saturated clothes.
